nodes.title: Proof: the counts ratio is the MLE
nodes.content:
Proof: The counts ratio is the MLE



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof — the counts ratio is the MLE.}}

\emph{Step 1: define the likelihood.} The \textbf{likelihood} is the probability of observing the data we actually saw, written as a function of the unknown parameter. Here the parameter is the transition matrix $\theta = \mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})$:\[ L(\mathbf{P};\, \text{data}) \;=\; \mathbb{P}\bigl(\text{data} \,\big|\, \mathbf{P}\bigr), \qquad \text{viewed as a function of } \mathbf{P}. \]

\emph{Step 2: factorise.} Condition on the fixed initial values $y_{k,0}$. Using (M2) i.i.d.\ trajectories, (M1) Markov property + chain rule, and homogeneity (so each one-step conditional is $p_{y_{k,t-1},\, y_{k,t}}$):\[ L(\mathbf{P};\, \underbrace{y_1, \dots, y_n)}_{\text{data from N indiv. eacn observed T times}} \;=\; \underbrace{\prod_{k=1}^{n}\,}_{\text{k individuals}} \underbrace{p_{y_{k,0}, y_{k,1}}\,}_{\text{whatever state the individaul visits}} p_{y_{k,1}, y_{k,2}} \cdots p_{y_{k,T-1}, y_{k,T}}. \]

\emph{Step 3: regroup by transition counts.} The same factor $p_{i,j}$ appears in the product once per observed transition $i \to j$ in the panel (obivously, just grouping probabilities!):\[ L(\mathbf{P};\, \text{data}) \;=\; \prod_{i=1}^{M}\prod_{j=1}^{M} \underbrace{p_{i,j}^{\, n_{i,j}}}_{g(T(x), \theta))}. \] So the statistic $T(x) = \{n_{i,j}\}$ is \textbf{jointly sufficient} for $\mathbf{P}$ 

\emph{Step 4: find MLE by maximise L wrt $p_{i,j}$ and you get: \[ \boxed{\hat p_{i,j} \;=\; \frac{n_{i,j}}{n_{i,+}}, \qquad i, j = 1, \dots, M.} \]

nodes.title: Asymptotics
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4.2 Asymptotic distributions.}}


**Preamble:** 
- Experiment, run 1 time, yes no: bernoulli -> run 10 times: binomial  --> CLT -> univariate gaussian (yes,no)
- Experiment, run 1 tine, many possible outcomes k: categorical (ni1, ni2..niM) -> run 10 times (10 individuals): multinomial ---> multivariate gaussian (k outcomes, you see a gaussian k dimensional cloud). Please notice that multinomial is just repeated bernoulli but with k states!

\textit{Setup for the Markov chain.} Let $\eta_h$ be the initial probability of state $h$ and $n_h(0)$ the number of individuals in state $h$ at $t = 0$. We study the behaviour of $\hat p_{i,j}$ as $n \to \infty$ under the assumption\[ \frac{n_h(0)}{n} \;\longrightarrow\; \eta_h, \qquad h = 1, \dots, M. \]Recall that the MLE of the $i$-th row of $\mathbf{P}$ is $(\hat p_{i,1}, \dots, \hat p_{i,M})$ with $\hat p_{i,j} = n_{i,j}/n_{i,+}$, and\[ (n_{i,1}, \dots, n_{i,M}) \;\sim\; \mathrm{Multinomial}(n_{i,+};\ p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,M}). \]Note: $n_{i,+}$ is itself random, since it depends on how often the panel visits state $i$.

\emph{Step 1} $\hat p_{ij}$ is just a ratio, by CLT is multivariate gaussian (many possible outcomes).


\emph{Step 2 --- handle the randomness of $n_{i,+}$.} Define the expected number of times state $i$ is visited per subject: \[ \varphi_i \;=\; \sum_{h=1}^{M} \eta_h \sum_{t=1}^{T} p^{(t-1)}_{h,\, i}, \]where $p^{(t-1)}_{h, i}$ is the probability of state $i$ at time $t-1$ given state $h$ at time $0$. So $n\, \varphi_i$ is the expected total number of observations in state $i$ over $t = 0, 1, \dots, T-1$, averaged over the initial distribution. Then\[ \frac{n_{i,+}}{n} \;\longrightarrow\; \varphi_i \quad \text{as } \quad n \to \infty, \qquad \text{so } n_{i,+} \approx n\, \varphi_i. \]
Concrete example to feel it: $T = 5$, all $p^{(t-1)}{h,i} = 0.3, \sum{t=1}^{5} 0.3 = 1.5.$ That's the expected number of times (out of 5) we visit state $i$ — perfectly consistent: 30% chance per period × 5 periods = expect 1.5 visits.

\textit{Step 3}. Conditional on $n_{i,+}$ known, standard multinomial-MLE theory gives, for $j, h = 1, \dots, M$, $j \neq h$,\[ \mathbb{E}(\hat p_{i,j}) = p_{i,j}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\hat p_{i,j}) = \frac{p_{i,j}(1 - p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(\hat p_{i,j},\ \hat p_{i,h}) = -\frac{p_{i,j}\, p_{i,h}}{n_{i,+}}, \] and an asymptotic multivariate Gaussian distribution for $(\hat p_{i,1}, \dots, \hat p_{i,M}) \approx \mathcal{N}_M\bigl(p_i,\ \Sigma_i\bigr)$. Approximate all with $\hat p_{-,-}$! 


\textit{Asymptotic confidence intervals.} A level-$(1-\alpha)$ CI for $p_{i,j}$ is\[ \boxed{\;\hat p_{i,j} \;\pm\; z_{\alpha/2}\,\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_{i,j}\,(1 - \hat p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}}\;} \]with $z_{\alpha/2}$ the $(1-\alpha/2)$-quantile of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ (e.g.\ $z_{0.025} \approx 1.96$ for $95\%$).

nodes.title: Hidden Markov  Models
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{HIDDEN MARKOV MODELS (HMM)}}

\begin{keydef}
\textbf{Hidden Markov Model (HMM).} An HMM is a discrete-time pair of stochastic processes
\[ \bigl(\, \underbrace{Y_t}_{\text{observation}},\; \underbrace{S_t}_{\text{latent}} \,\bigr)_{t \ge 1}, \quad \text{starting at } S_0, \]
where the distribution that generates the observation $Y_t$ depends on the state of an underlying \emph{unobserved} state process $(S_t)$, such that:

$\bullet$ \textbf{(1) Latent homogeneous Markov state process.} $(S_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a homogeneous Markov chain on a finite state space $\mathcal{S} = \{1, \dots, M\}$ with initial distribution $\pi$ and transition matrix $\mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})$, $p_{i,j} = P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i)$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{(2) Conditional independence of the observations.} Given the latent path $(S_t)_{t \ge 0}$, the $Y_t$'s are conditionally independent and each $Y_t$ depends only on $S_t$.

\textbf{Equivalently,} the law of an HMM is fully specified by:
\[ S_0 \;\sim\; \pi, \qquad S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \;\sim\; \text{Categorical}(p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,M}), \qquad Y_t \mid S_t = j \;\sim\; p(y_t \mid \theta_j^*), \]
i.e.\ an initial distribution on the states, a discrete transition matrix for the hidden chain, and an emission distribution per state (parameters $\{\theta_j^*\}_{j=1}^M$).
\end{keydef}

\emph{When is it useful?} ARMA-type models assume stationarity. HMMs are tailored for \emph{non-stationary} series with change points / regime switches — e.g.\ speech recognition, business-cycle detection, unbounded-count series (Poisson observation "number of calls in one hour"  ) where the rate switches between states. Why not modelign it with a poisson? becasse poisson is st mean and variance coincide (do not want this constraint)

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Toy 3-regime Gaussian HMM.}} A simple example with three regimes is\[ Y_t = \begin{cases} \mu_1 + e_t & \text{if } S_t = 1, \\ \mu_2 + e_t & \text{if } S_t = 2, \\ \mu_3 + e_t & \text{if } S_t = 3, \end{cases} \qquad e_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). \]More compactly, $Y_t = \mu_{S_t} + e_t$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The "equation" of the hidden chain (3-regime example).}} For this toy example, $K = 3$ and the state space is $\mathcal{S} = \{1, 2, 3\}$. The conditional law of $S_t$ given $S_{t-1} = i$ is the categorical distribution given by row $i$ of $\mathbf{P}$:
\[ S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \;\sim\; \text{Categorical}\bigl(p_{i,1},\, p_{i,2},\, p_{i,3}\bigr), \]
i.e.\ $P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i) = p_{i,j}$, plus the initial law $S_0 \sim \pi = (\pi_1, \pi_2, \pi_3)$. This is the "equation" of the hidden Markov chain --- once you draw $S_t$ from this categorical, the observation is $Y_t = \mu_{S_t} + e_t$.

\textit{Note:} the observed process $(Y_t)$ itself is generally \emph{not} Markov — observing $Y_{t-1}$ does not pin down $S_{t-1}$. The Markov property lives at the level of the \emph{hidden} chain.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Specifying the law of an HMM.}} It follows that the probability law of the hidden Markov process $\bigl((S_t, Y_t)\bigr)_{t \ge 0}$ is specified by assigning:

$\bullet$ the \textbf{initial distribution} of the hidden state: $S_0 \sim \pi$ on $\mathcal{S} = \{1, \dots, M\}$, that is $(p_0(1), ... , p_0(k))$; 

$\bullet$ the \textbf{transition matrix} of the hidden chain: $A = \mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})_{i,j \in \mathcal{S}}$ with $p_{i,j} = P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i)$;

$\bullet$ the \textbf{emission distributions} $\{p(y \mid s) : s \in \mathcal{S}\}$, one per state

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{DAG view of an HMM — reading conditional independence.}}
see figure!

nodes.title: Example emission matrices
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE EMISSION MATRICES}}

Recall the emission distributions are the probability distribution of the observable variable $Y_t$ given the state $S_t = j$, for $j = 1, \dots, K$. Two standard cases.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Discrete (non-parametric) case.}} Suppose $Y_t$ takes values in the finite set $\{1, \dots, M\}$. The general (non-parametric) form of the emission distribution in state $j$ is

\[ Y_t \mid S_t = j \;\sim\; \bigl(\, \underbrace{P(Y_t = 1 \mid S_t = j)}_{b_{j,1}}, \;\dots,\; \underbrace{P(Y_t = i \mid S_t = j)}_{b_{j,i}}, \;\dots,\; \underbrace{P(Y_t = M \mid S_t = j)}_{b_{j,M}} \,\bigr), \]

i.e.\ we let $P(Y_t = y \mid S_t = j) \equiv b_{j,y}$, $y = 1, \dots, M$. Collecting the emission probabilities $b_{j,y}$ in the \emph{emission matrix}

\[ B = [b_{j,y}]_{j=1,\dots,K;\; y=1,\dots,M}, \]

we use the compact notation $\phi = (A, B, \pi)$ to represent the HMM. Specification of the HMM then requires choosing the number of states $K$ and the probability matrices $A$, $B$ and the initial vector $\pi$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. Parametric case --- Poisson emissions.}} In other cases one may want a parametric emission distribution, so that $Y_t \mid S_t = j \sim p(\,\cdot \mid \theta_j^*)$, $j = 1, \dots, K$. For example, for the earthquakes data (unbounded counts), one could assume
\[ Y_t \mid (S_t = j) \;\sim\; \text{Poisson}(\theta_j^*), \]
that is, at state $j$, $Y_t$ has a Poisson distribution with parameter $\theta_j^*$. Note how the parameter can switch across states!

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this fixes the plain-Poisson defects.}} A single Poisson forces (i) mean $=$ variance, (ii) no serial dependence. Letting the rate \emph{switch} with a Markov chain breaks all three:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Different mean and variance per regime.} Within state $j$, both equal $\lambda_j^*$, but across regimes they differ --- a "quiet" state has small mean \emph{and} small variance, an "active" one has large mean \emph{and} large variance.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Autocorrelation.} Sticky regimes ($p_{j,j}$ near $1$) mean neighbouring $Y_t$'s likely share the same rate, so
\[ \text{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t+h}) \;=\; \text{Cov}(\lambda_{S_t}^*, \lambda_{S_{t+h}}^*) \;>\; 0. \]
No additive $\epsilon$ needed --- the dependence comes from persistence of the hidden chain.

nodes.title: Specification
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. MODEL SPECIFICATION}}

Choosing the number $K$ of hidden states is a natural first question. In some applications, $K$ is suggested by knowledge of the domain under study. In other cases, one can try a few different values of $K$ and compare the performance of the resulting models.

nodes.title: Estimation
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. ESTIMATION OF THE UNKNOWN PARAMETERS}}

We estimate the unknown parameters $\phi = (A, B, \pi)$ of an HMM by \emph{maximum likelihood}. Focus on the \emph{discrete non-parametric case}: $Y_t \in \{1, \dots, M\}$, latent states $S_t \in \{1, \dots, K\}$.

The likelihood is the joint probability of the observed sequence $y_{1:T}$, read as a function of $\phi$.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 1 --- Marginalise the hidden path.}} Since $S_{0:T}$ takes \emph{some} path in every realisation, the events $\{S_{0:T} = s_{0:T}\}$ partition the sample space. By the law of total probability:
\[ L(\phi \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; P(Y_{1:T} = y_{1:T} \mid \phi) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{a sum over all possible b}}\; \sum_{s_{0:T} \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} P(Y_{1:T} = y_{1:T},\, S_{0:T} = s_{0:T} \mid \phi) \underbrace{=}_{\text{chain rule}} \underbrace{P(Y_{1:T} \mid S_{0:T},\, \phi)}_{(\mathrm{A})\,\text{ obs.\ given path}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{P(S_{0:T} \mid \phi)}_{(\mathrm{B})\,\text{ path probability}}. \]

Explaining notation: The sum is over all $K^{T+1}$ possible state paths $(s_0, s_1, \dots, s_T)$. So we have T+1 terms, each can take K values. 


\emph{A direct evaluation of such joint probability may be involved, because the temporal dependence of the process $(Y_t)$ may be complex. Fortunately, after extracting latents, we can exploit the conditional independence structure of the HMM.} We derive it step by step.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 3 --- Compute $(\mathrm{A})$ via conditional independence of observations.}} Chain rule then HMM emission assumption (each $Y_t$ depends only on its own $S_t$ given the path):
\[ (\mathrm{A}) \;=\; \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(Y_t = y_t \mid S_t = s_t,\, \phi) \;=\; \prod_{t=1}^{T} b_{s_t, y_t}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 4 --- Compute $(\mathrm{B})$ via Markov property of the chain.}} Chain rule then Markov assumption (each $S_t$ depends only on $S_{t-1}$):
\[ (\mathrm{B}) \;=\; P(S_0 \mid \phi) \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(S_t \mid S_{t-1},\, \phi) \;=\; \pi_{s_0} \prod_{t=1}^{T} p_{s_{t-1}, s_t}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 5 --- Combine.}} Multiply $(\mathrm{A})$ and $(\mathrm{B})$ inside the sum:
\[ \boxed{\; L(\phi \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \sum_{s_{0:T} \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} \underbrace{\pi_{s_0}}_{\text{initial}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T} p_{s_{t-1}, s_t}}_{\text{transitions}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T} b_{s_t, y_t}}_{\text{emissions}}  \;=\; \sum_{s_{0:T}} \pi_{s_0}\, p_{s_0, s_1}\, b_{s_1, y_1}\, p_{s_1, s_2}\, b_{s_2, y_2}\, \cdots\, p_{s_{T-1}, s_T}\, b_{s_T, y_T}. \qquad (2) \;} \]


\emph{Exercise.} Write the expression of the likelihood in the discrete parametric case, assuming that the emission distribution is Poisson.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Maximisation.}} The MLE is $\hat\phi = \arg\max_{\phi} L(\phi \mid y_{1:T})$. Direct numerical maximisation is feasible but expensive; in practice, the EM algorithm (\emph{Baum-Welch} for HMMs) is the standard iterative procedure.

nodes.title: Decoding
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. DECODING}}

Estimate the latent state sequence $s_{1:T}$ given observed $y_{1:T}$ (treat $s_0$ as fixed, and $\phi$ as known or replaced by its MLE).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Local criterion.}} For each $t = 1, \dots, T$, pick the marginally most likely state:
\[ s_t^* \;=\; \arg\max_s \gamma_t(s), \qquad \gamma_t(s) \;\equiv\; P(S_t = s \mid y_{1:T}, \phi). \]
\emph{Issue.} The resulting sequence $s_{1:T}^*$ may include zero-probability transitions ($p_{i,j} = 0$), making the global path infeasible.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Global criterion --- Viterbi.}} Find the path that maximises the joint conditional probability:
\[ \max_{s_{0:T}} P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T, \phi). \]
Given the data, and the parameters, what is the most likely hidden state? 

This conditional probability can be computed using Bayes theorem. However, we can more easily exploit the computations already carried out for the MLE. Notice that
\[ \begin{aligned} & P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T,\, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi) \\ & \underbrace{=}_{\text{chain rule}} P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T, \phi)\, P(Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi), \end{aligned} \]
where the latter factor on the right-hand side does not depend on $s_{0:T}$. Therefore, maximising the conditional joint probability with respect to $s_{0:T}$ is equivalent to maximising the joint probability $P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T,\, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi)$ wrt phi. Now we need to optimize the same thing by $S_{0:T}$

nodes.title: Example — Nile river
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE --- Nile river data}}

In LAB 2 we consider a few examples on the use of HMMs with R, using the R package \texttt{depmixS4}.

The following example considers the \emph{Nile river data}, available in R, which provides the measurements of the annual flow of the Nile river in the period 1871--1970. We envisage a change point around the year 1898, when the construction of the first dam in Aswan was started. This suggests to fit an HMM with $K = 2$ states --- so $(S_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a Markov chain with state space $\mathcal{S} = \{1, 2\}$ --- and to assume a \emph{Gaussian emission distribution} with state-specific parameters:
\[ \begin{aligned} Y_t \mid S_t = 1 &\;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_1^*, \sigma_1^*), \\ Y_t \mid S_t = 2 &\;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_2^*, \sigma_2^*), \end{aligned} \]
where the (unknown) parameters are $\theta_1^* = (\mu_1^*, \sigma_1^*)$ and $\theta_2^* = (\mu_2^*, \sigma_2^*)$. We also fix the initial distribution as
\[ \pi \;=\; \bigl(\, \pi_1 = 0, \;\; \pi_2 = 1 \,\bigr). \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The "equation" of the hidden chain.}} For this 2-state chain, the conditional law of $S_t$ given $S_{t-1} = i$ is the categorical distribution given by row $i$ of $\mathbf{P}$:
\[ S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \;\sim\; \text{Categorical}\bigl(p_{i,1}, p_{i,2}, \dots, p_{i,K}\bigr), \]
i.e.\ $P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i) = p_{i,j}$, plus the initial law $S_0 \sim \pi$. This is the "equation" of a Markov chain.





\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MLE of the transition matrix.}} The maximum likelihood estimates of the transition matrix, provided by \texttt{depmixS4}, are
\begin{tabular}{c|cc} $t-1 \backslash t$ & $1$ & $2$ \\ \hline $1$ & $1.00$ & $0.00$ \\ $2$ & $0.04$ & $0.97$ \end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MLE of the emission parameters.}} The MLEs of the parameters $\theta_j^*$ are
\[ \hat\theta_1^* = (\hat\mu_1^*, \hat\sigma_1^*) = (850.57,\; 124.45), \qquad \hat\theta_2^* = (\hat\mu_2^*, \hat\sigma_2^*) = (1097.15,\; 133.75). \]

\emph{Remark.} Reporting the MLEs is not enough. One should also provide the \textbf{standard errors} of the MLEs (possibly approximated by bootstrap techniques), or at least their \emph{asymptotic} standard errors, obtained from the asymptotic properties of MLEs. The computation of the standard errors for the MLEs of the fitted HMM, using the R package \texttt{depmixS4}, is illustrated in Lab 2.

nodes.title: Exercise — weather/activity filtering (state is unobserved)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXERCISE --- Filtering: weather $\to$ activity}}

\textbf{Setup.} A person's daily activity depends on the weather, which is hidden. We observe only the activity.

$\bullet$ Hidden $\mathcal{S} = \{1 = \text{sunny},\, 2 = \text{rainy}\}$ ($K = 2$), observed $\mathcal{Y} = \{1 = \text{walk},\, 2 = \text{shop},\, 3 = \text{clean}\}$ ($M = 3$).

$\bullet$ Initial $\pi = (P(S_1 = \text{sunny}), P(S_1 = \text{rainy})) = (0.6,\, 0.4)$.

\textbf{Transition matrix} $A$ (rows = state at $t-1$, columns = state at $t$):
\begin{tabular}{c|cc} $t-1 \backslash t$ & sunny & rainy \\ \hline sunny & $0.7$ & $0.3$ \\ rainy & $0.4$ & $0.6$ \end{tabular}

\textbf{Emission matrix} $B$ (rows = state, columns = activity):
\begin{tabular}{c|ccc} $S_t \backslash Y_t$ & walk & shop & clean \\ \hline sunny & $0.6$ & $0.3$ & $0.1$ \\ rainy & $0.1$ & $0.4$ & $0.5$ \end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The universal recipe (forward algorithm).}} Define
\[ \alpha_t(j) \;:=\; P(S_t = j,\; y_{1:t}) \quad\text{(joint "score": data observed so far AND being in state $j$ now)}. \]
One rule for every step:
\[ \boxed{\; \alpha_t(j) \;=\; \underbrace{b_{j, y_t}}_{\text{today's evidence}} \cdot \underbrace{\sum_{i} \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, p_{i,j}}_{\text{yesterday's belief, pushed forward through } A}, \qquad \alpha_1(j) \;=\; \pi_j\, b_{j, y_1}. \;} \]
\emph{In words:} transition the old belief through $A$, then weight by today's emission. Past observations are never thrown away --- they live inside $\alpha_{t-1}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(a) After $y_1 = \text{walk}$.}} No transition needed yet (start of chain):
\[ \alpha_1(\text{sunny}) = \pi_{\text{sunny}}\, b_{\text{sunny, walk}} = 0.6 \cdot 0.6 = 0.36, \qquad \alpha_1(\text{rainy}) = 0.4 \cdot 0.1 = 0.04. \]
Walking is far more compatible with sunny ($0.6$ vs $0.1$) $\Rightarrow$ score ratio $9{:}1$ in favour of sunny.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(b) After $y_2 = \text{shop}$.}}

\emph{Predict $S_2$ from history:} push $\alpha_1$ through $A$:
\[ \text{pred}_2(\text{sunny}) = 0.36 \cdot 0.7 + 0.04 \cdot 0.4 = 0.268, \qquad \text{pred}_2(\text{rainy}) = 0.36 \cdot 0.3 + 0.04 \cdot 0.6 = 0.132. \]
\emph{Weight by today's emission:}
\[ \alpha_2(\text{sunny}) = 0.268 \cdot 0.3 = 0.0804, \qquad \alpha_2(\text{rainy}) = 0.132 \cdot 0.4 = 0.0528. \]
Shopping is mildly more compatible with rainy ($0.4$ vs $0.3$), pulling the belief from $9{:}1$ down to roughly $1.5{:}1$; sunny stays ahead because the chain is sticky ($p_{\text{sunny}, \text{sunny}} = 0.7$).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Take-aways.}}

$\bullet$ Two-step recipe at every $t$: (1) push the old belief through $A$ to get the predicted prior; (2) multiply by the emission to fold in today's evidence.

$\bullet$ $\alpha_t(j) = P(S_t = j, y_{1:t})$ is a \emph{joint}, not a posterior. Their relative magnitudes already tell you which state is more likely; summing them gives the data likelihood $P(y_{1:t}) = \sum_j \alpha_t(j)$ for free.

$\bullet$ This is exactly the \emph{forward algorithm} --- the engine inside HMM likelihood evaluation, filtering, and (with a small modification: $\max$ instead of $\sum$) Viterbi decoding.

nodes.title: State space models (SSM)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{STATE SPACE MODELS (SSM)}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{One-line intuition.}}  A latent process $(\theta_t)$ evolves Markovianly in its state space, and each observation $Y_t$ is drawn from a distribution determined only by the current state.

So the time series you see is the output of a dynamic system  (the latent procss) + some random disturbances. What is nice is that the underlying dynamic system can have a trends, seasonal componetns, regressive components etc so there is a lot of flesibilty. On top of this they have a very nice probabilityic structure (embed in everything you are doing). 




\begin{keydef}
\textbf{State-space model (SSM).} An SSM is a dyamic system of stochastic processes
\[ \bigl(\, \underbrace{Y_t}_{\text{observation}},\; \underbrace{\theta_t}_{\text{latent}} \,\bigr)_{t \ge 1}, \quad \text{starting at } \theta_0, \]
where the distribution that generates the observation $Y_t$ depends on the state of an underlying \emph{unobserved} state process $(\theta_t)$, such that:

$\bullet$ \textbf{(1) Latent Markov state process.} $(\theta_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a Markov process with continuous state space $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p$, initial distribution $\pi$ and transition kernel $f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$. (In HMMs the state space is discrete $\mathcal{S} = \{1, \dots, M\}$ and the kernel is a matrix; here $\Theta$ is continuous.)

$\bullet$ \textbf{(2) Conditional independence of the observations.} Given the latent path $(\theta_t)_{t \ge 0}$, the $Y_t$'s are conditionally independent and each $Y_t$ depends only on $\theta_t$ \[ p(y_t \mid \theta_{0:t}, y_{1:t-1})= p(y_t \mid \theta_t) \]                                                                                                                         
\textbf{Equivalently,} the law of an SSM is fully specified by:
\[ \theta_0 \;\sim\; \pi, \qquad \theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \;\sim\; f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1}), \qquad Y_t \mid \theta_t \;\sim\; f(y_t \mid \theta_t), \]
i.e.\ an initial law on the state, a transition kernel for the state, and an emission kernel for the observation.
\end{keydef}



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Two layers of inference: don't confuse them.}}

The transition kernel $f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$ plays \emph{two different roles}, depending on which question you are asking.

$\bullet$ \textbf{(A) Model ingredient (input).} When the model is fully known, $f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$ is \emph{given}. You use it \emph{inside} the algorithms (it's the engine of the recursive Bayes update: "carry yesterday's belief forward through the transition"), but it is not the \emph{target} of inference. The four canonical inference tasks --- filtering, smoothing, prediction, decoding --- all assume the model is known and use the transition kernel as an ingredient.

$\bullet$ \textbf{(B) Unknown parameter (target).} When the model has unknown parameters $\phi$, the transition becomes $f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1}; \phi)$ and you genuinely want to learn it from data. In HMMs, $\phi$ contains the entire matrix $\mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})$. This is a \emph{separate} inference question:

- \emph{Observed Markov chain:} count transitions, $\hat p_{i,j} = n_{i,j} / n_{i,+}$ (the panel-survey exercises).
- \emph{Hidden Markov chain (HMM):} the chain is unobserved, so counting is not possible. Use MLE. \emph{Workflow.} Parameter inference first ($\hat\phi$ from the data), then plug $\hat\phi$ in and do state inference. The four canonical tasks live in the second layer; the transition kernel is itself a \emph{target} only when you're in the first layer.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Specialisations / next topics.}}

$\bullet$ The four canonical inference tasks --- \emph{filtering} $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})$, \emph{smoothing} $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T})$ , \emph{prediction} $f(\theta_{t+h}, Y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$ --- all use only the joint factorisation above. The Kalman filter, forward algorithm, Viterbi and particle filter are just \emph{efficient ways to do the recursive Bayes update} on that joint.

Note Smoothing for HMM: applies the "local" criterion. For HMM we used viterbi, the global criterion (so smoothign is more or less decoding).

nodes.title: Bayesian statistics
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{BAYESIAN STATISTICS --- Bayes' rule, derivation and intuition}}

You forecast the next value to be A. But you want to deal with uncertainty... the soltuon is probability

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The goal.}} We want to know
\[  P(A \mid B) \;=\; \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \]
i.e.\emph{"after seeing evidence $B$, how likely is hypothesis $A$?"}. 
\emph{The problem.} The joint $P(A \cap B)$ is usually hard to compute directly. Bayes' rule is the trick to express it in terms of quantities we can compute.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{From the definition of conditional probability.}} For two events $A, B$,
\[ P(A \mid B) \;=\; \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \qquad P(B \mid A) \;=\; \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}. \]
merge out the intersection: 
\[ \underbrace{P(A \mid B)}_{\text{posterior: belief in } A \text{ \emph{after} seeing } B} \;=\; \frac{\overbrace{P(B \mid A)}^{\text{likelihood: how compatible } B \text{ is with } A}\, \cdot \overbrace{P(A)}^{\text{prior: belief in } A \text{ \emph{before} seeing } B}}{\underbrace{P(B)}_{\text{evidence: marginal probability of } B}}. \]

Bayes is a form of learning from experience! 


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Key reformulation --- the "evidence multiplier".}} Rewrite Bayes as
\[ P(A \mid B) \;=\; P(A) \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\frac{P(B \mid A)}{P(B)}}_{\text{evidence multiplier}}. \]

Clearly the denominator is a normalization. That is this event happens with 3% probablity in eenral, when A is active, 4% so this evidence is aligned with A being active. Notcie, aybe youhave prior of 90% that somebody is guilty then you get a very irrelevatn test that with 5% probability fires guilty in generla, and ot tis  guy it fired 5.1%.d oes htis mea tha tthe probabioty of him biegn guilty is now 5.1%? no! you had other proofs that had ocmposed that 90% and this extra evidence is a tiny little new proof in favour of him beign gy8itly




\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why Bayes' rule is brilliant.}} The genuine insight is the \emph{change of perspective}:
\[ \underbrace{P(A \cap B)}_{\text{hard to compute directly}} \;\;\longleftrightarrow\;\; \underbrace{P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A)}_{\text{both easy: a model + a prior}}. \]
You see, an hard co-occurence problem has been simplified to a conditional probablity (derivable from an experiment) and a prior. 



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Concrete example --- medical test.}}

$\bullet$ Disease prevalence: $P(D) = 0.01$.

$\bullet$ True positive rate: $P(+ \mid D) = 0.99$.

$\bullet$ False positive rate: $P(+ \mid \neg D) = 0.05$.

\emph{Question:} A patient tests positive. What is $P(D \mid +)$?

Bayes:
\[ P(D \mid +) \;=\; \frac{P(+ \mid D)\, P(D)}{P(+)}. \]
Denominator (law of total probability):
\[ P(+) \;=\; P(+ \mid D)\, P(D) + P(+ \mid \neg D)\, P(\neg D) \;=\; 0.99 \cdot 0.01 + 0.05 \cdot 0.99 \;=\; 0.0594. \]
So
\[ P(D \mid +) \;=\; \frac{0.99 \cdot 0.01}{0.0594} \;\approx\; 0.167. \]

\emph{Reading.} Even with a "99\% accurate" test, a positive result means only $\approx 17\%$ chance of having the disease --- because the disease is rare to start with. The prior $P(D) = 0.01$ is so small that the evidence multiplier $P(+ \mid D)/P(+) = 0.99 / 0.0594 \approx 16.7$ only pushes the posterior to $0.01 \times 16.7 \approx 0.17$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Core Bayesian idea.}} Evidence must be interpreted \emph{relative to the baseline frequency}. Rare priors require strong evidence to overturn.

nodes.title: Bayesian vs frequentist inference
Lindley Paradox
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Lindley's paradox --- when the two frameworks loudly disagree.}}

A famous case where frequentist and Bayesian conclusions \emph{conflict} on the same data, especially when $n$ is large.

\textbf{Setup.} Test $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ vs $H_1: \theta \ne \theta_0$, with sample mean $\hat\theta$ near (but not exactly equal to) $\theta_0$.

\textbf{Frequentist machinery.} The test statistic
\[ z = \frac{\hat\theta - \theta_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} \]
contains $\sqrt{n}$. So for any fixed deviation $\hat\theta - \theta_0 \ne 0$, $z$ grows without bound as $n \to \infty$, and the p-value $\to 0$. With enough data, the test \emph{rejects} $H_0$ for any deviation, no matter how small.

\textbf{Bayesian machinery.} Under $H_1$, place a prior $\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$. The Bayes factor is
\[ \text{BF}_{01} \;=\; \frac{p(y \mid H_0)}{p(y \mid H_1)}, \qquad p(y \mid H_1) \;=\; \int p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta \mid H_1)\, d\theta. \]
The integral averages over \emph{all} $\theta$ in the prior --- including the many values that do not fit $\hat\theta$. With a wide prior, only a tiny sliver near the data has high likelihood; the rest contributes almost nothing. So $H_1$ is \emph{penalised for being a vague hypothesis}: the marginal likelihood is dilute. In large samples this Occam penalty wins unless $H_1$ actually concentrates mass near the observed value.

\textbf{Concrete numbers.} $\sigma = 1$, $\theta_0 = 0$, $\hat\theta = 0.002$, $n = 1{,}000{,}000$, $\tau = 1$:
\[ z \;=\; 2 \;\Rightarrow\; p \;\approx\; 0.045  (\text{frequentist rejects at 5\%}), \]
\[ \text{BF}_{01} \;\approx\; \tau \sqrt{n} \cdot e^{-z^2/2} \;=\; 1000 \cdot e^{-2} \;\approx\; 135  (\text{Bayes factor: data 135}\times \text{ more likely under } H_0). \]

\emph{Same data, opposite conclusions:} frequentist rejects $H_0$, Bayesian strongly supports $H_0$.

\textbf{Why the disagreement?} The two methods answer \emph{different questions}.

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist}: "How extreme is the data assuming $H_0$?" With huge $n$, even practically negligible deviations look extreme.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian}: "Which hypothesis predicts the data better, on average?" The vague $H_1$ pays an Occam penalty for spreading prior mass over values that no longer fit.

\textbf{Intuition in one line.}
\[ \text{Frequentist asks: \emph{is the true } \theta \text{ exactly } \theta_0?} \Longleftrightarrow \text{Bayesian asks: \emph{is the data well explained by } \theta_0 \text{ vs by an averaged-over } H_1?} \]

\textbf{Practical message.}

$\bullet$ For \emph{small to moderate $n$} the two frameworks usually agree numerically.

$\bullet$ For \emph{very large $n$} (high-frequency finance, genomics, particle physics), p-values reject everything --- Bayes factors are preferred for model selection.

$\bullet$ This is not a numerical fluke: it is a real difference in what "evidence" means in each framework. Use the framework whose question matches what you actually want to know.

nodes.title: Derivation: Prediction
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{PREDICTION --- how Bayesian concepts give us all the formulas}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Intro.}} \emph{Where does the predictive density come from?} By the definition of a conditional density (chain rule applied to the joint of the first $t + h$ observations):
\[ f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \frac{f(y_{1:t},\, y_{t+h})}{f(y_{1:t})}. \]
Natural starting point, BUT SAME AS BEFORE: \emph{both} densities on the right are usually intractable directly --- use the trick.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{General version (textbook posterior predictive, $h$-step ahead).}} For observed data $y_{1:t}$, future observation $y_{t+h}$, and contemporaneous latent state $\theta_{t+h}$:
\[ \boxed{\; f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) \;\underbrace{=}_{(*)}\; \int f(y_{t+h},\, \theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h} \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{Bayes on the integrand}}\; \int f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t},\, \theta_{t+h})\, f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h} \;=\; \int f(y_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h})\, \underbrace{f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})}_{\text{filter + predict}}\, d\theta_{t+h}. \;} \]

$(\ast)$ Marginalisation: ask yourself --- \emph{when $y$ takes this value, what value does $\theta$ take?} --- and average. The integration variable must match what's varying in the integrand.

\emph{Reading.} \textbf{KEY:} For each candidate value of the contemporaneous state $\theta_{t+h}$, the emission gives a forecast $f(y_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h})$; we average these forecasts, weighted by how plausible each $\theta_{t+h}$ is given the data we have already seen ($f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$, the predicted-state distribution).

nodes.title: Proof for the closed form versions of Ct and mt in the fixed theta case
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{WORKED EXAMPLE --- RW + noise with fixed hidden state}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setup.}} The local-level state-space model with state-noise variance fixed to $W = 0$ (so $w_t = 0$ a.s.\ and the state is constant: $\theta_t = \theta_0 \equiv \theta$ for all $t$):

$\bullet$ \emph{State equation (degenerate random walk):} $\theta_t \;=\; \theta_{t-1},\qquad \theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, C_0).$

$\bullet$ \emph{Observation equation:} $Y_t \;=\; \theta + \varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2),\quad \{\varepsilon_t\} \perp \theta.$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Goal.}} Compute the posterior $f(\theta \mid y_{1:n})$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Reminder --- Gaussian density (kernel form).}} A $\mathcal{N}(m,\, C)$ density evaluated at $x$ (mean $m$, variance $C$) is
\[ \mathcal{N}(x;\, m,\, C) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi C}} \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{(x - m)^2}{2 C}\Bigr). \]
For matching coefficients, we will repeatedly use the kernel-in-$\theta$ form (everything not involving $\theta$ goes into the normalising constant):
\[ \mathcal{N}(\theta;\, m,\, C) \;\stackrel{\theta}{\propto}\; \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[\theta^2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{C} \;-\; 2\theta \cdot \tfrac{m}{C}\bigr]\Bigr). \]

\begin{tabular}{l|l|l}
Step & Non-recursive (batch) & Recursive (one-step-at-a-time) \\
\hline
\emph{Bayes setup} & iid factorises the likelihood: \;$f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \propto \prod_{t=1}^{n} f(y_t \mid \theta) \cdot \pi(\theta).$ &\;$f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \propto f(y_n \mid \theta_n) \cdot f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n-1}) $ with $f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n-1}) = \mathcal{N}(m_{n-1}, C_{n-1})$:  \\
\hline
\emph{Step 1 - plug in Gaussians} & $f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \propto \exp\!\bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{t=1}^{n}(y_t - \theta)^2\bigr) \cdot \exp\!\bigl(-\tfrac{(\theta - m_0)^2}{2 C_0}\bigr).$ & $f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \propto \exp\!\bigl(-\tfrac{(y_n - \theta_n)^2}{2\sigma^2}\bigr) \cdot \exp\!\bigl(-\tfrac{(\theta_n - m_{n-1})^2}{2 C_{n-1}}\bigr).$ \\
\hline
\emph{Step 2 - collect $\theta^2,\, \theta$ terms} & $f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \stackrel{\theta}{\propto} \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl[\theta^2\bigl(\tfrac{1}{C_0} + \tfrac{n}{\sigma^2}\bigr) - 2\theta\bigl(\tfrac{m_0}{C_0} + \tfrac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\bigr)\Bigr]\Bigr).$ & $f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \stackrel{\theta_n}{\propto} \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl[\theta_n^2\bigl(\tfrac{1}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\bigr) - 2\theta_n\bigl(\tfrac{m_{n-1}}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{y_n}{\sigma^2}\bigr)\Bigr]\Bigr).$ \\
\hline
\emph{Step 3 - match the kernel} $(m, C)$ & $\tfrac{1}{C_n} = \tfrac{1}{C_0} + \tfrac{n}{\sigma^2}; \quad m_n = C_n\bigl(\tfrac{m_0}{C_0} + \tfrac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\bigr).$ \;Equivalently: \;$C_n = \tfrac{C_0\, \sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + n\, C_0}, \quad m_n = \tfrac{\sigma^2\, m_0 + n\, C_0\, \bar y}{\sigma^2 + n\, C_0}.$ & $\tfrac{1}{C_n} = \tfrac{1}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}; \quad m_n = C_n\bigl(\tfrac{m_{n-1}}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{y_n}{\sigma^2}\bigr).$ \;Equivalently: \;$C_n = \tfrac{C_{n-1}\, \sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + C_{n-1}},\quad m_n = \tfrac{\sigma^2\, m_{n-1} + C_{n-1}\, y_n}{\sigma^2 + C_{n-1}}.$ \\
\hline
\emph{Result} & $\boxed{\; \theta \mid y_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_n,\, C_n) \;}$ with the closed-form $(m_n, C_n)$ above. & $\boxed{\; \theta_n \mid y_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_n,\, C_n) \;}$ obtained by iterating the recursion $n$ times from $(m_0, C_0)$. \\
\end{tabular}

nodes.title: Parameter Estimation
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{PARAMETER ESTIMATION}}

Estimate the \emph{fixed}, time-invariant constants $\phi$ of the model from data $y_{1:T}$. Two routes: \emph{maximum likelihood} (frequentist) or \emph{Bayesian inference}.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Parameter vs latent state --- the key distinction.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Latent state $\theta_t$:} dynamic, unobserved, lives at each time. Targets: $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})$ (filtering), $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T})$ (smoothing). Handled by recursive Bayes (Kalman / forward--backward).

$\bullet$ \emph{Parameter $\phi$:} static, unknown, shared across all $t$. Targets: $\hat\phi$ (MLE) or $f(\phi \mid y_{1:T})$ (posterior). Single quantity, not a trajectory.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Examples.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{iid Gaussian:} $\phi = (\mu, \sigma^2)$.

$\bullet$ \emph{AR($p$):} $\phi = (\phi_1, \dots, \phi_p, \sigma^2)$.

$\bullet$ \emph{HMM:} $\phi = (P,\, \{\theta_j^*\},\, \pi)$ --- transition matrix, emission parameters, initial distribution.

$\bullet$ \emph{DLM (time-invariant):} $\phi = (F, G, V, W)$, plus $(m_0, C_0)$ for the initial state.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{How to}}

You mazimize the likelihood: 
\[ \hat\phi_{\text{MLE}} ;=; \arg\max_\phi, f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi), \qquad f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi) ;=; \int f(y_{1:T},, \theta_{0:T} \mid \phi), d\theta_{0:T}. \]
$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist}: maximise over $\phi$ to get the MLE $\hat\phi$. 
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Identifiability.}}

Two parameter values $\phi_1 \neq \phi_2$ may give the SAME likelihood for every possible dataset: $f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi_1) = f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi_2)\ \forall y_{1:T}$. Then the $\arg\max$ is not unique --- the model is \emph{not identifiable}. Two standard tie-breakers:

$\bullet$ \emph{Parsimony.} Prefer the simpler model (fewer parameters, simpler structure). Occam's razor: when two models fit the data equally well, pick the smaller.

$\bullet$ \emph{Sparsity.} Prefer parameter vectors with many \emph{zero} entries. ``Most coefficients are inactive.'' Operationalised by adding a penalty: e.g.\ LASSO $\hat\phi = \arg\max_\phi \log f(y \mid \phi) - \lambda \sum_j |\phi_j|$ pushes small $\phi_j$ exactly to zero. Useful when you believe only a few covariates truly matter.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Frequentist CI for MLE --- iid case.}}

\emph{Setup.} $X_1, \dots, X_n \stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} p_\theta$, $\theta \in \Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Likelihood and log-likelihood:
\[ L_n(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(X_i), \qquad \ell_n(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(X_i). \]
\emph{MLE:} $\hat\theta_n = \arg\max_\theta \ell_n(\theta)$. \emph{Score = derivative of log-likelihood;} setting it to zero gives the MLE first-order condition $\ell_n'(\hat\theta_n) = 0$.

\emph{Fisher information $I_1(\theta)$ of one observation:}
\[ I_1(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_\theta\!\left[\left(\frac{d \log p_\theta(X)}{d\theta}\right)^2\right] \;=\; -\,\mathbb{E}_\theta\!\left[\frac{d^2 \log p_\theta(X)}{d\theta^2}\right]. \]
\emph{Reading:} measures how sharply the log-likelihood is curved around $\theta$ on average. Sharper curvature $\Rightarrow$ more information $\Rightarrow$ tighter estimate.

\emph{Total Fisher information for $n$ iid observations:}
\[ I_n(\theta) \;=\; n \cdot I_1(\theta) \qquad \text{(iid summation)}. \]

\emph{Asymptotic normality of the MLE (Cram\'er; regularity conditions: correct model, identifiability, smooth $p_\theta$, finite $I_1$).}
\[ \sqrt{n}\,\bigl(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0\bigr) \;\xrightarrow{d}\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(0,\; I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr). \]
\emph{Hence for $n$ large:}
\[ \hat\theta_n \;\overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}\; \mathcal{N}\!\Bigl(\theta_0,\; \tfrac{1}{n\, I_1(\theta_0)}\Bigr) \;=\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\theta_0,\; I_n(\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr). \]
\emph{Variance reading:} the MLE's variance is the inverse Fisher information --- the Cram\'er--Rao lower bound is attained asymptotically (MLE is \emph{asymptotically efficient}).

\emph{Plug-in for $\theta_0$ (Slutsky):} consistency $\hat\theta_n \xrightarrow{P} \theta_0$ lets us replace $I_n(\theta_0)$ with $I_n(\hat\theta_n)$.

\emph{$(1-\alpha)$ Wald confidence interval:}
\[ \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha}(\theta_0) \;=\; \hat\theta_n \;\pm\; z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{I_n(\hat\theta_n)}} \;=\; \hat\theta_n \;\pm\; \frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}}{\sqrt{n\, I_1(\hat\theta_n)}}. \]
For 95\%: $z_{0.975} = 1.96$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Multivariate case ($\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$).}}

The scalar Fisher info becomes the $d \times d$ \emph{Fisher information matrix} --- you cannot use a single second derivative; you need the full \emph{Hessian} of the log-likelihood:
\[ I_1(\theta) \;=\; -\,\mathbb{E}_\theta\!\bigl[\nabla^2_\theta \log p_\theta(X)\bigr] \quad\text{(a $d \times d$ matrix, the negative expected Hessian)}. \]
$I_n(\theta) = n\, I_1(\theta)$ as before. Asymptotic normality:
\[ \sqrt{n}\,\bigl(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0\bigr) \;\xrightarrow{d}\; \mathcal{N}_d\!\bigl(0,\; I_1(\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr) \;\Longrightarrow\; \hat\theta_n \;\overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}\; \mathcal{N}_d\!\bigl(\theta_0,\; I_n(\theta_0)^{-1}\bigr). \]
Wald CI for component $\theta_j$ uses the $(j,j)$ entry of the \emph{inverse} Fisher matrix:
\[ \mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha}(\theta_{0,j}) \;=\; \hat\theta_{n,j} \;\pm\; z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\sqrt{\bigl[I_n(\hat\theta_n)^{-1}\bigr]_{jj}}. \]

\emph{Practical note.} In code one usually computes the \emph{observed} information $\hat I_n = -\nabla^2 \ell_n(\hat\theta_n)$ (the actual Hessian at the MLE), then inverts it for standard errors --- avoids having to evaluate the expectation analytically.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Putting parameter uncertainty into prediction.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist plug-in.} Take $\hat\phi$, then compute $f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}, \hat\phi)$ by the rules above. \emph{Pretends $\hat\phi$ is the truth} --- forecast bands too narrow. 

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian posterior predictive.} Integrate out $\phi$:
\[ f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \int f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}, \phi)\, f(\phi \mid y_{1:T})\, d\phi. \]
This is just \emph{Bayes' rule applied twice}: once to get the filtered/predicted state distribution given $\phi$, then again to integrate out the parameter. Forecast bands honestly account for parameter uncertainty.

nodes.title: SSM flexibility — no stationarity required
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SSM FLEXIBILITY --- why no stationarity requirement}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why ARMA cannot fit a non-stationary series.}} ARMA models a process with \emph{constant} parameters $(\phi_i, \theta_j, \sigma^2)$. A model with constant parameters can only describe data whose statistical properties are themselves constant in time: constant mean, constant variance, autocovariance depending only on the lag. That is exactly the definition of weak stationarity.

If the data has a trend (mean drifting upward), seasonality (mean cycling), or changing volatility (variance growing), there is \emph{no choice} of constants $(\phi_i, \theta_j, \sigma^2)$ that can reproduce it --- because constants cannot represent a moving target. 

\emph{Practical recipe with ARMA:} first remove the non-stationary features (differencing $\to$ ARIMA, deseasonalising $\to$ SARIMA, detrending) so that the residual series is stationary; only then fit ARMA.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why SSMs do not.}} An SSM separates two concerns:
\[ \theta_t = G_t \theta_{t-1} + w_t  (\text{state evolves}), \qquad Y_t = F_t \theta_t + v_t  (\text{observation snapshot}). \]
The state $\theta_t$ itself is allowed to be \emph{non-stationary}; the observation inherits that non-stationarity. Non-stationary behaviour is encoded directly inside $\theta_t$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Flexibility: stack components in the state vector.}} The state can be assembled from independent blocks, each contributing its own structure:

$\bullet$ \emph{Trend block:} $\mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_{1,t}$, $\beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + w_{2,t}$ --- a level $\mu_t$ that drifts with a slope $\beta_t$ that itself drifts.

$\bullet$ \emph{Seasonal block:} $s_t + s_{t-1} + \dots + s_{t-S+2} = w_t$ (dummy form), or trigonometric Fourier components --- periodicity built in.

$\bullet$ \emph{Regression block:} $\alpha_t = \alpha_{t-1} + w_t$ multiplied by a covariate $x_t$ in $F_t$ --- regression coefficient evolving in time.

$\bullet$ \emph{AR / autoregressive block:} state contains lagged values, transition is the companion matrix.

Stacked: $\theta_t = (\mu_t,\, \beta_t,\, s_t,\, s_{t-1},\, \dots,\, \alpha_t,\, \dots)^\top$, and $Y_t = F_t \theta_t + v_t$ picks the relevant linear combination. Each block evolves independently, and $Y_t$ is their joint output plus noise.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The cleanest contrast.}}

\begin{tabular}{l|l|l} & ARMA & SSM \\ \hline Models & correlation structure of $Y_t$ directly & generative mechanism producing $Y_t$ \\ Parameters & constant in $t$ & can be time-varying \\ State / memory & implicit in lagged $Y$'s & explicit in $\theta_t$ \\ Trend, seasonality & must be removed first & encoded in $\theta_t$ \\ Non-stationary data & not supported & natively supported \end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Intuition --- model the system, not the symptoms.}} ARMA describes how $Y_t$ correlates with its own past, summarised by a few constants; that only works if those correlations don't drift. SSMs describe \emph{what is producing} $Y_t$ --- a latent dynamical system whose own evolution can have trend, drift, seasonal swings, regime switches. Whatever pattern of correlations comes out is a \emph{consequence} of the chosen state dynamics, not a constraint on the model class.

\emph{Exam relevance.} The May 2021 CO\textsubscript{2} question asks exactly this: trend + seasonality in the raw data, can you use a DLM \emph{without} preliminary transformation? Answer: \textbf{yes}, because trend and seasonal components live inside the state and are estimated jointly with everything else --- no detrending, no deseasonalising required.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Aside --- if you let ARMA's parameters drift, you get an SSM.}} The cleanest way to see SSM as the strict superset of ARMA is to let the ARMA coefficients become time-varying.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Step 1 --- make ARMA time-varying.} Replace constants with functions of $t$:
\[ Y_t \;=\; \phi_1(t)\, Y_{t-1} + \dots + \phi_p(t)\, Y_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1(t)\, \varepsilon_{t-1} + \dots, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_t^2). \]
On its own this is ill-posed: infinitely many parameters, unidentifiable from finite data.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Step 2 --- give the coefficients their own evolution.} Treat $\phi_i(t), \theta_j(t), \sigma_t^2$ as random processes --- typically random walks:
\[ \phi_i(t) \;=\; \phi_i(t-1) + \eta_{i,t}, \qquad \eta_{i,t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, q_i). \]

$\bullet$ \textbf{Step 3 --- stack into a state vector.} Let
\[ \theta_t \;=\; \bigl(\underbrace{Y_t, Y_{t-1}, \dots, Y_{t-p+1}}_{\text{lagged values}},\; \underbrace{\phi_1(t), \dots, \phi_p(t)}_{\text{time-varying coeffs}},\; \dots\bigr)^\top. \]
Both the lagged data and the coefficients now live inside the state. The state equation handles their joint evolution; the observation equation $Y_t = F_t \theta_t + v_t$ picks the right linear combination. This is a DLM (linear Gaussian SSM); the products $Y_{t-1}\, \phi_1(t)$ are handled either by treating $Y_{t-1}$ as a known regressor (giving a \emph{dynamic regression / TVP-regression DLM}) or via a nonlinear SSM (extended/unscented Kalman, particle filter).

nodes.title: Example SSMs
Examples 1 & 2: RW and RW + drift (A and B)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLES 1 \& 2 --- random walk, random walk with drift (A: directly observed; B: SSM lift).}}

See the \emph{Example SSMs hub} for the canonical DLM template, the specialisation tree, and the worked 2$\times$2 matrix example.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 1 --- Simple random walk.}}

\textbf{(A) Directly observed.} A player starts with capital $y_0 > 0$. Each step: gain $+1$ w.p.\ $p$, loss $-1$ w.p.\ $1-p$. With $Z_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} (\pm 1)$:
\[ Y_t \;=\; Y_{t-1} + Z_t \;=\; y_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{t} Z_i. \]
$Z_t$ iid and independent of past $Y$'s $\Rightarrow$ Markov. With $y_0 = 0$, $E[Z_t] = 0$: $E[Y_t] = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = t\sigma^2$ --- variance grows linearly, so the walk is \textbf{non-stationary}. \emph{Continuous-time limit} (small steps in rapid succession): \textbf{Brownian motion}. The recursion works for any iid $Z_t$, not just $\pm 1$.

\textbf{(B) SSM lift --- RW + noise (local-level model).} \emph{Specialise the DLM template:} $G = 1,\; F = 1,\; W = \sigma_z^2,\; V = \sigma_\varepsilon^2$:
\begin{keydef}
\textbf{Random walk + noise (local-level model).}

\emph{State equation (latent):} $\;\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} + z_t,\quad z_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_z^2),\quad \theta_0$ given.

\emph{Observation equation:} $\;y_t = \theta_t + \varepsilon_t,\quad \varepsilon_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2),\quad \{\varepsilon_t\} \perp \{z_s\}.$
\end{keydef}

The \emph{signal-to-noise ratio} $\sigma_z^2 / \sigma_\varepsilon^2$ controls how much $y_t$ reveals about $\theta_t$:

$\bullet$ $\sigma_\varepsilon^2 \to 0$: $y_t = \theta_t$ --- recover Part (A) (state observed exactly).

$\bullet$ $\sigma_z^2 \to 0$: state frozen at $\theta_0$, $y_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\theta_0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)$ --- iid noise around a constant.

\emph{Moments (with $\theta_0 = 0$):} $E[y_t] = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(y_t) = t\sigma_z^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2$ --- non-stationary.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 2 --- Random walk with drift.}}

\textbf{(A) Directly observed.} Same recursion as Example 1, but now the increments have non-zero mean: $\mu := E[Z_t] \ne 0$ (the \emph{drift}), $\sigma^2 := \mathrm{Var}(Z_t)$. Decompose into trend + zero-mean walk:
\[ Y_t \;=\; \underbrace{(y_0 + t\mu)}_{\text{deterministic trend}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{t} (Z_i - \mu)}_{\text{zero-mean random walk}}. \]
\emph{Non-stationary:} $E[Y_t] = y_0 + t\mu$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = t\sigma^2$.

\textbf{(B) SSM lift --- RW + drift + noise.} see in table

nodes.title: Example 3: AR(1) (A and B)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 3 --- AR(1), continuous-state Markov (A: directly observed; B: SSM lift).}}

See the \emph{Example SSMs hub} for the canonical DLM template, the specialisation tree, and the worked 2$\times$2 matrix example.

\textbf{(A) Directly observed.} Discrete-time Markov process on $\mathbb{R}$:
\[ Y_t \;=\; \varphi\, Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). \]
Three regimes:

$\bullet$ $\varphi = 1$: \emph{random walk} --- the Gaussian, continuous-state version of Example 1 ($\pm 1 \to \varepsilon_t \in \mathbb{R}$, state space $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$).

$\bullet$ $|\varphi| < 1$: \emph{stationary}, mean-reverting toward $0$, stationary variance $\sigma^2/(1-\varphi^2)$.

$\bullet$ $|\varphi| > 1$: \emph{explosive} --- variance grows exponentially.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof: $|\varphi| < 1$ $\Rightarrow$ weakly stationary.}} Unroll the recursion from $Y_0$:
\[ Y_t \;=\; \varphi^t Y_0 \;+\; \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \varphi^k\, \varepsilon_{t-k}. \]
We check the three conditions of weak stationarity (assume $\varepsilon_t$ iid with mean $0$, variance $\sigma^2$, and $\varepsilon_t \perp Y_0$).

\emph{1.\ Constant mean.}
\[ E[Y_t] \;=\; \varphi^t\, E[Y_0] \;+\; \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \varphi^k\, \underbrace{E[\varepsilon_{t-k}]}_{=\,0} \;=\; \varphi^t\, E[Y_0]. \]
With $E[Y_0] = 0$ (e.g.\ start from the stationary distribution): $E[Y_t] = 0$ for all $t$. Otherwise $\varphi^t E[Y_0] \to 0$ geometrically (asymptotic mean stationarity). \quad $\checkmark$

\emph{2.\ Constant, finite variance.} By independence of shocks and $Y_0$:
\[ \mathrm{Var}(Y_t) \;=\; \varphi^{2t}\, \mathrm{Var}(Y_0) \;+\; \sigma^2 \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \varphi^{2k}. \]
The geometric series $\sum_{k\ge 0} \varphi^{2k}$ converges iff $\varphi^2 < 1$, i.e.\ $|\varphi| < 1$, with limit $1/(1-\varphi^2)$. Starting from $\mathrm{Var}(Y_0) = \sigma^2/(1-\varphi^2)$:
\[ \gamma(0) \;:=\; \mathrm{Var}(Y_t) \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{1-\varphi^2} \qquad \text{for all } t. \quad \checkmark \]

\emph{3.\ Autocovariance depends only on lag $h$.} For $h \ge 0$:
\[ \gamma(h) \;:=\; \mathrm{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t+h}) \;=\; \mathrm{Cov}\!\left(Y_t,\; \varphi^h Y_t + \sum_{j=1}^{h} \varphi^{h-j} \varepsilon_{t+j}\right) \;=\; \varphi^h\, \gamma(0). \]
No $t$-dependence. \quad $\checkmark$

\emph{Autocorrelation:} $\rho(h) = \gamma(h)/\gamma(0) = \varphi^{|h|}$ --- decays geometrically, sign alternates if $\varphi < 0$.

\emph{Why the other regimes fail.} $|\varphi| = 1$: $\sum \varphi^{2k} = t$, so $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = t\sigma^2 \to \infty$. $|\varphi| > 1$: $\varphi^{2t} \to \infty$, variance explodes. In both cases condition (2) fails.

Continuous-state Markov processes are the building block for SSMs.

\textbf{(B) SSM lift --- AR(1) as a degenerate DLM.} \emph{Specialise the DLM template:} $G = \varphi,\; F = 1,\; W = \sigma^2,\; V = 0$, with $\theta_t := Y_t$:
\[ \theta_t = \varphi\, \theta_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad Y_t = \theta_t. \]
The "latent" state isn't really hidden ($V = 0 \Rightarrow Y_t$ reveals it exactly), but it formally satisfies the DLM template. A non-degenerate lift would set $V = \sigma_\nu^2 > 0$ (analogous to Examples 1B and 2B), giving an AR(1) corrupted by measurement noise.

nodes.title: Example 4: AR(2) and AR(p) via state augmentation
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 4 --- AR($p$) via state augmentation (book-faithful form, DLMwR pp.\ 112--113).}}

See the \emph{Example SSMs hub} for the canonical DLM template and the worked 2$\times$2 matrix example.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Book convention.}} DLMwR uses an auxiliary-component augmentation (eqs.\ 3.23--3.25), \emph{not} the naive "stack lagged $Y$" form. The book explicitly notes (p.\ 113) that "$F_t$ of a DLM cannot depend on past values of the observations," ruling out lagged-$Y$ as state components.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{First: the AR(2) special case ($p = 2$).}}

\emph{Model.} $Y_t = \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t$, $\varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$.

\emph{(1) State.} $\theta_t = (\theta_{1,t},\, \theta_{2,t})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^2$ with $\theta_{1,t} = Y_t$; $\theta_{2,t}$ is an auxiliary component (not equal to a lagged $Y$ directly).

\emph{(2) Component equations.}
\[ \theta_{1,t} = \phi_1\, \theta_{1,t-1} + \theta_{2,t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \theta_{2,t} = \phi_2\, \theta_{1,t-1}. \]

\emph{(3) Matrix state eq.}
\[ \begin{pmatrix} \theta_{1,t} \\ \theta_{2,t} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 & 1 \\ \phi_2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{G} \begin{pmatrix} \theta_{1,t-1} \\ \theta_{2,t-1} \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_t \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad W = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \]

\emph{(4) Obs eq.} $Y_t = F\, \theta_t = (1,\, 0)\, \theta_t = \theta_{1,t}$ (degenerate: $V = 0$).

\emph{Verification --- recover the AR(2) recursion.} From the first component equation:
\[ Y_t = \theta_{1,t} = \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \theta_{2,t-1} + \varepsilon_t. \]
But from the second component (one step back): $\theta_{2,t-1} = \phi_2\, \theta_{1,t-2} = \phi_2 Y_{t-2}$. Substitute:
\[ Y_t = \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t. \;\checkmark \]
The auxiliary state $\theta_{2,t}$ acts as a "delayed echo" $\phi_2 Y_{t-1}$ that arrives at the next step.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{General AR($p$) --- 4-step DLM template (book companion form).}}

\emph{(1) State.} $\theta_t = (\theta_{1,t},\, \dots,\, \theta_{p,t})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^p$, with $\theta_{1,t} = Y_t$; $\theta_{2,t}, \dots, \theta_{p,t}$ are auxiliary components (delayed echoes, \emph{not} lagged observations).

\emph{(2) Component equations.}
\[ \theta_{1,t} = \phi_1\, \theta_{1,t-1} + \theta_{2,t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \quad \theta_{j,t} = \phi_j\, \theta_{1,t-1} + \theta_{j+1,t-1} \;\text{ for } j = 2, \dots, p-1, \quad \theta_{p,t} = \phi_p\, \theta_{1,t-1}, \]
with $\varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$.

\emph{(3) Matrix state equation.}
\[ \begin{pmatrix} \theta_{1,t} \\ \theta_{2,t} \\ \vdots \\ \theta_{p-1,t} \\ \theta_{p,t} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \phi_2 & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & & \ddots & \\ \phi_{p-1} & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \\ \phi_p & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{G} \begin{pmatrix} \theta_{1,t-1} \\ \theta_{2,t-1} \\ \vdots \\ \theta_{p-1,t-1} \\ \theta_{p,t-1} \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_t \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad W = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2,\, 0,\, \dots,\, 0). \]

\emph{(4) Observation equation.} $Y_t = F\, \theta_t + v_t = (1, 0, \dots, 0)\, \theta_t = \theta_{1,t}$, $F = (1, 0, \dots, 0)$, $V = 0$ (degenerate --- state observed exactly).

\emph{Reading.} The $\phi$'s sit in the \emph{first column} of $G$ (not the first row). The super-diagonal of 1's "shifts" auxiliary components, so each $\theta_{j,t-1}$ becomes a delayed contribution to $\theta_{1,\cdot}$ at the next step.

\emph{Why not lagged-$Y$ form?} Many textbooks use the "naive" companion $G$ with $\phi$'s in the first row and $\theta_t = (Y_t, Y_{t-1}, \dots, Y_{t-p+1})^\top$ --- mathematically equivalent but uses observations as state components, which the strict DLM definition (DLMwR p.\ 113) forbids. The book's auxiliary form satisfies the DLM constraint while still encoding the AR($p$) dynamics.

nodes.title: Probability vs Likelihood
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Probability vs likelihood --- one formula, two readings.}}

The expression $P(B \mid A)$ is \emph{literally} the same number whether you call it a probability or a likelihood. There is no different formula and no proportionality involved:
\[ L(A; B) \;=\; P(B \mid A). \]
The only thing that changes is what you keep fixed and what you treat as the argument:

$\bullet$ \emph{Probability reading.} $A$ is fixed, $B$ varies. Evaluating $P(B \mid A)$ tells you how likely each potential outcome $B$ is, under the assumed hypothesis $A$. Used for \emph{forward prediction}.

$\bullet$ \emph{Likelihood reading.} $B$ is fixed at the data we actually observed, $A$ varies. Now $P(B \mid A)$ is read as a function of $A$ --- it scores how well each candidate hypothesis explains the observed $B$. This is the reading in the Bayes context. 

depends on what data you observe and what is unknowns! (or you have both)

nodes.title: Derivation: Filtering
nodes.content:
NOW WE USE BAYES RULE:


Recall: $y_{1:T}$ is shorthand for $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_T)$, the joint of all observations.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Filtering (state estimation)} $\;\;f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})$.} \emph{What is the state today, given everything observed up to today?}

Kalman derived it in a totally different way, it did a recursive least stare estimation (regression). Later, this derivation, that is fully bayesian came. Note how you (1) start by applyign the bayes rule and (2) we treat $\theta_t$ as random and compute its full posterior distribution $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})$, not just a point estimate or a sampling distribution of an estimator

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CASE 1 --- iid observations given $\theta$ (the textbook conjugate setting).}}

Treat $y_{1:t}$ as a \emph{single blob} $B$. Apply vanilla Bayes $f(A \mid B) \propto f(B \mid A)\, f(A)$ with $A = \theta$:
\[f(\theta \mid y_{1:t})\;\propto\;f(y_{1:t} \mid \theta)\;\cdot\;f(\theta) \underbrace{=}_{\text{ iid }}  \Bigl[\prod_{s=1}^{t} f(y_s \mid \theta)\Bigr] \cdot f(\theta). \]
Note that without iid you cannto simplfy the first term, note it has nothing to do with markov, \emph{When does this case apply?}
$\bullet$ \textbf{Necessary condition --- $\theta$ static.} If $\theta$ varied with $t$, the marginal of $Y_t \mid \theta_t$ would change with $t$ --- not \emph{identically distributed}, so not iid.\quad \emph{Exception:} if the $\theta_t$ are themselves iid in time (this is not a random walk, this is a fixed theta + some gaussian noise, different at each step (not accumulated)).

$\bullet$ \textbf{Not sufficient --- $\theta$ static does \emph{not} imply iid given $\theta$.} Counter-example: AR(1) with $\theta = (\phi, \sigma^2)$ static. Even after knowing $\theta$, $Y_t$ depends on $y_{t-1}$ through the AR equation $Y_t = \phi Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$. The likelihood factors via the chain rule as $\prod_t f(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1}, \theta)$, \emph{not} as a clean $\prod_t f(y_t \mid \theta)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CASE 2 --- Otherwise (time-varying state $\theta_t$, or temporal dependence).}}
Use the trick and remember Bayes with background ($A = \theta_t$, $B = y_t$, $C = y_{1:t-1}$):
\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_t,\, y_{1:t-1}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{f(y_t \mid \theta_t,\, y_{1:t-1})}_{ f(y_t \mid \theta_t)} \;\cdot\; f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}). \]
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Deriving the predicted prior $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$ (one line, three rules).}}

\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;\underbrace{=}_{(1)}\; \int f(\theta_t,\, \theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})\, d\theta_{t-1} \;\underbrace{=}_{(2)}\; \int f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1},\, y_{1:t-1})\, f(\theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})\, d\theta_{t-1} \;\underbrace{=}_{(3)}\; \int \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})}_{\text{transition}}\, \underbrace{f(\theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{\text{yesterday's posterior}}\, d\theta_{t-1}. \]

\textbf{(1)} \emph{Marginalisation (law of total probability):} introduce $\theta_{t-1}$ by integrating over it.

\textbf{(2)} \emph{Chain rule} $f(A \cap B \mid C) = f(A \mid B,\, C)\, f(B \mid C)$ with $A = \theta_t$, $B = \theta_{t-1}$, $C = y_{1:t-1}$.

\textbf{(3)} \emph{Markov property of the latent process:} given $\theta_{t-1}$, the next state $\theta_t$ doesn't depend on past observations, so $f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1},\, y_{1:t-1}) = f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$.

\emph{Interpretation.} Today's predicted state distribution $=$ average (integral) of the transition probabilities from yesterday to today, weighted by yesterday's posterior --- "where you were yesterday."

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The filtering recursion (Case 2, full).}}
\[ \boxed{\; f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{f(y_t \mid \theta_t)}_{\text{single new emission}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{\substack{\text{predicted prior} \\ \text{(integrate transition} \\ \text{against yesterday's posterior)}}}. \;} \]
\emph{Step pattern.} \textbf{Predict} (transition forward) $\to$ \textbf{update} (Bayes with $y_t$). Repeat at each $t$.

nodes.title: Smoothing and decoding
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SMOOTHING (and a note on DECODING) --- DLMwR Sec.\ 2.7.4 / pp.\ 60--63.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Smoothing:} $\boxed{\,\pi(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T}),\quad t < T\,}$ --- \emph{past} state given \emph{ALL} the data, including observations after $t$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Kalman smoother --- one backward pass, two possible outputs.}}

\emph{Inputs (run forward filter first and store).} Filtering moments $(m_t, C_t)$ and predicted-state moments $(a_{t+1}, R_{t+1})$ for every $t = 0, \dots, T$.


\emph{Backward pass} for $t = T-1, T-2, \dots, 0$ --- choose one of two modes:

\textbf{(A) Analytical marginals} $\theta_t \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(s_t, S_t)$ (Prop.\ 2.4, p.\ 61):
\[ s_t \;=\; m_t + J_t\, (s_{t+1} - a_{t+1}), \qquad S_t \;=\; C_t - J_t\, (R_{t+1} - S_{t+1})\, J_t^\top. \]
\emph{The smoother gain (shared by both outputs):}
\[ \boxed{\; J_t \;=\; C_t\, G_{t+1}^\top\, R_{t+1}^{-1}. \;} \]
$J_t$ is the regression coefficient of $\theta_t$ on $\theta_{t+1}$ in their joint Gaussian distribution --- the backward analog of the Kalman gain.

\emph{Reading $s_t$ component-wise.} $s_t$ is just the vector of \emph{component-wise expected values} of the state given all data:
\[ s_t \;=\; E[\theta_t \mid y_{1:T}]. \]
If, e.g., $\theta_t = (\alpha_t,\, \beta_t)^\top$ (described by the component equations $\alpha_t = \dots$, $\beta_t = \dots$), then
\[ s_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} E[\alpha_t \mid y_{1:T}] \\ E[\beta_t \mid y_{1:T}] \end{pmatrix}. \]
Each entry of $s_t$ is the posterior mean of the corresponding state component conditional on the full data record. Same for $S_t$: the $(i,i)$ entries are the marginal variances $\mathrm{Var}(\theta_{i,t} \mid y_{1:T})$, off-diagonals the covariances.

\emph{Initialise at $t = T$:} the last time-point has no future, so smoothing $=$ filtering: $s_T = m_T,\; S_T = C_T$, or sample $\theta_T \sim \mathcal{N}(m_T, C_T)$.

nodes.title: Posterior mean and precision
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Posterior precision $1/C_n$.}} The precision \emph{adds}:
\[ \underbrace{\frac{1}{C_n}}_{\text{posterior precision}} \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{C_0}}_{\text{prior precision}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{n}{\sigma^2}}_{\text{data precision}}. \]
The lower the variance of Cn th ebetter! Because both terms are non-negative, $1/C_n \ge 1/C_0$ always --- the posterior is \emph{always} at least as precise as the prior. Even poor-quality data (large $\sigma^2$) adds some information, just less of it. Sharper data ($\sigma^2$ small) or more data ($n$ large) makes the posterior sharper.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Posterior mean $m_n$ as a weighted average.}} Rewrite $m_n$:
\[ m_n \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{1/C_0}{1/C_0 + n/\sigma^2}}_{\text{prior weight}} \cdot m_0 \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{n/\sigma^2}{1/C_0 + n/\sigma^2}}_{\text{data weight}} \cdot \bar y. \]
$m_n$ is a convex combination of the \emph{prior mean} $m_0 = E[\theta]$ and the \emph{sample mean} $\bar y$, with weights proportional to the respective precisions (frequentist would just have used the sample mean).

nodes.title: SSM filtering and prediction
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CHEATSHEET --- inference formulas, side-by-side (Case A vs Case B)}}

\emph{Notation.} \textbf{Case A} = iid observations given a static $\theta$ (textbook conjugate setting; no time evolution of the parameter). \textbf{Case B} = SSM with time-varying latent state $\theta_t$ (Markov dynamics, here illustrated with the local-level / RW + noise model).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Models in equation form.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Case A (static $\theta$, iid Gaussian observations).}
\[ \theta \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0,\, C_0); \qquad Y_{t+1} \;=\; \theta + \varepsilon_{t+1}, \qquad \varepsilon_{t+1} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, V). \]

$\bullet$ \textbf{Case B (DLM, local-level / RW + noise).}
\[ \theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0,\, C_0); \qquad \theta_{t+1} \;=\; \theta_t + w_{t+1}, \quad w_{t+1} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, W); \qquad Y_{t+1} \;=\; \theta_{t+1} + \varepsilon_{t+1}, \quad \varepsilon_{t+1} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, V). \]
\begin{tabular}{l|l|l}
Topic & \textbf{Case A} (iid / static $\theta$) & \textbf{Case B} (DLM / linear-Gaussian SSM) \\
\hline
\emph{1. Filtering: posterior of state given data up to now} & $f(\theta \mid y_{1:T}) \;\propto\; \Bigl[\prod_{s=1}^{T} f(y_s \mid \theta)\Bigr] \cdot f(\theta)$ & $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) \;\propto\; f(y_t \mid \theta_t)\, \cdot\, f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$, \;with \;$f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) = \int f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})\, f(\theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})\, d\theta_{t-1}$. You can prove the joint is notrmal gaussian. \\
\hline
\emph{2. One-step state prediction} & $f(\theta \mid y_{1:T})$ unchanged (static state) & $f(\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}) = \int f(\theta_{t+1} \mid \theta_t)\, f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_t$ \;(single predict step) \\
\hline
\emph{3. $h$-step state prediction} & $f(\theta \mid y_{1:T})$ unchanged (static state) & $f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) = \int f(\theta_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h-1})\, f(\theta_{t+h-1} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h-1}$ \;(iterate the one-step predict $h$ times) \\
\hline
\emph{4. $h$-step observation prediction} & $f(y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T}) = \int f(y_{T+h} \mid \theta)\, f(\theta \mid y_{1:T})\, d\theta$ & $f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) = \int f(y_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h})\, f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h}$ \\
\hline
\emph{5a. Gaussian posterior / state forecast $\theta_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T}$} & $\theta \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_T,\, C_T)$ with $C_T = \tfrac{C_0\, V}{V + T\, C_0}$, \;$m_T = \tfrac{V\, m_0 + T\, C_0\, \bar y}{V + T\, C_0}$. \;$\theta_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} = \theta \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_T, C_T)$ \emph{(state is constant, all horizons identical)}. & \emph{Posterior:} $\theta_T \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_T, C_T)$. \;\emph{1-step:} $\theta_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(a_{T+1}, R_{T+1})$ with $a_{T+1} = G\, m_T$, $R_{T+1} = G\, C_T\, G^\top + W$. \;\emph{$h$-step (iterate predict):} $\theta_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(a_{T+h}, R_{T+h})$ with $a_{T+h} = G\, a_{T+h-1} = G^h\, m_T$ and $R_{T+h} = G\, R_{T+h-1}\, G^\top + W = G^h\, C_T\, (G^h)^\top + \sum_{j=0}^{h-1} G^j\, W\, (G^j)^\top$. \\
\hline
\emph{5b. One-step Gaussian predictive $Y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}$} & $Y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(f_{T+1},\, Q_{T+1})$ with $f_{T+1} = m_T$, $Q_{T+1} = C_T + V$. \;Variance $=$ state posterior uncertainty $+$ obs noise. & $Y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(f_{T+1},\, Q_{T+1})$ with $f_{T+1} = F\, a_{T+1} = m_T$, $Q_{T+1} = F\, R_{T+1}\, F^\top + V = C_T + W + V$. \;Variance $=$ state posterior uncertainty $+$ new state innovation $+$ obs noise. \\
\hline
\emph{5c. $h$-step Gaussian predictive $Y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T}$} & $Y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(f_{T+h},\, Q_{T+h})$ with $f_{T+h} = m_T$, $Q_{T+h} = C_T + V$. \;(Same as 5b for all $h$ because the state is fixed.) & $Y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(f_{T+h},\, Q_{T+h})$ with $f_{T+h} = m_T$, $Q_{T+h} = C_T + h\, W + V$. \;Forecast bands fan out linearly in $h$. \\
\hline
\emph{5d. Filter update --- prediction-error correction form} & $m_t = m_{t-1} + K_t\, e_t$, \;$C_t = (1 - K_t)\, C_{t-1}$, \;where $e_t = y_t - m_{t-1}$ (innovation), $K_t = C_{t-1} / (C_{t-1} + V)$ (Kalman gain). \;Note $a_t = m_{t-1}$, $R_t = C_{t-1}$ (no predict step since $W = 0$). & $m_t = a_t + K_t\, e_t$, \;$C_t = R_t - K_t F\, R_t = (I - K_t F)\, R_t$, \;where $a_t = G\, m_{t-1}$, $R_t = G\, C_{t-1}\, G^\top + W$ (predict), \;$f_t = F\, a_t$, $Q_t = F\, R_t\, F^\top + V$, \;$e_t = y_t - f_t$ (innovation), \;$K_t = R_t\, F^\top\, Q_t^{-1}$ (Kalman gain). \\
\end{tabular}

\emph{Footnote on what these symbols mean.} Every $m_t, C_t, a_{t+1}, R_{t+1}, f_{t+1}, Q_{t+1}$ in the table is just a (conditional) expectation or variance:
\[ m_t = E[\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}], \;\; C_t = \mathrm{Var}(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}); \quad a_{t+1} = E[\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}], \;\; R_{t+1} = \mathrm{Var}(\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}); \quad f_{t+1} = E[Y_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}], \;\; Q_{t+1} = \mathrm{Var}(Y_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}). \]
The "Kalman formulas" in each row are just the application of $E$ and $\mathrm{Var}$ to the state and observation equations (using linearity and independence of the noise terms).
