\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Worked examples --- applying rows 5a + 5c at horizon $h$ (symbolic).}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Example I --- scalar $G = 2$.}}

\emph{Setup.} $\theta_t = 2\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t,\quad w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, W)$;\quad $Y_t = \theta_t + \varepsilon_t,\quad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, V)$.

\emph{(5a) State forecast at $T + h$.}
\[ a_{T+h} \;=\; G^h\, m_T \;=\; 2^h\, m_T, \qquad R_{T+h} \;=\; G^{2h}\, C_T + W \sum_{k=0}^{h-1} G^{2k} \;=\; 4^h\, C_T + W\, \tfrac{4^h - 1}{3}. \]
\[ \theta_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\Bigl(2^h\, m_T,\;\; 4^h\, C_T + W\, \tfrac{4^h - 1}{3}\Bigr). \]

\emph{Proof of the $R_{T+h}$ form (unroll the state $h$ steps).} From $\theta_t = G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t$:
\[ \theta_{T+h} \;=\; G^h\, \theta_T \;+\; \sum_{j=0}^{h-1} G^j\, w_{T+h-j}. \]
The current state $\theta_T$ is multiplied by $G^h$; each future shock $w_{T+k}$ ($k = 1, \dots, h$) is carried forward $h - k$ further steps, contributing weight $G^{h-k} = G^j$ (with $j = h - k$). Taking variance conditional on $y_{1:T}$ (using independence of $\theta_T$ and the shocks, and independence of the shocks across $t$):
\[ R_{T+h} \;=\; \mathrm{Var}(\theta_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; G^h\, C_T\, (G^h)^\top \;+\; \sum_{j=0}^{h-1} G^j\, W\, (G^j)^\top, \]
which in the scalar case with $G = 2$ becomes $4^h\, C_T + W \sum_{j=0}^{h-1} 4^j = 4^h C_T + W\, \tfrac{4^h-1}{3}$ (geometric series).

\emph{(5c) $Y_{T+h}$ predictive.}
\[ f_{T+h} \;=\; F\, a_{T+h} \;=\; 2^h\, m_T, \qquad Q_{T+h} \;=\; F^2\, R_{T+h} + V \;=\; 4^h\, C_T + W\, \tfrac{4^h - 1}{3} + V. \]
\[ Y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\Bigl(2^h\, m_T,\;\; 4^h\, C_T + W\, \tfrac{4^h - 1}{3} + V\Bigr). \]

\emph{Reading.} Forecast variance \textbf{explodes geometrically} ($\sim 4^h$) because $|G| > 1$ amplifies state variance every step.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Example II --- $2 \times 2$ $G$ (local linear trend: state $=$ level $+$ slope).}}

\emph{Setup.} $\theta_t = (\mu_t,\, \beta_t)^\top$;\quad $G = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$;\quad $F = (1,\, 0)$;\quad $W = \mathrm{diag}(W_\mu,\, W_\beta)$;\quad $V$ scalar. Filtered: $m_T = (m_\mu,\, m_\beta)^\top$,\quad $C_T = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}C_{\mu\mu} & C_{\mu\beta} \\ C_{\mu\beta} & C_{\beta\beta}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. Note $G^h = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & h \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.

\emph{(5a) State forecast at $T + h$.}
\[ a_{T+h} \;=\; G^h\, m_T \;=\; \begin{pmatrix}1 & h \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}m_\mu \\ m_\beta\end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix}m_\mu + h\, m_\beta \\ m_\beta\end{pmatrix}. \]
\[ R_{T+h} \;=\; G^h\, C_T\, (G^h)^\top + \sum_{k=0}^{h-1} G^k\, W\, (G^k)^\top. \]
\[ \theta_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}_2(a_{T+h},\, R_{T+h}). \]

\emph{(5c) $Y_{T+h}$ predictive.}
\[ f_{T+h} \;=\; F\, a_{T+h} \;=\; m_\mu + h\, m_\beta, \qquad Q_{T+h} \;=\; F\, R_{T+h}\, F^\top + V \;=\; [R_{T+h}]_{1,1} + V. \]
Notice how you care just about the variance of the first row.
\[ Y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(m_\mu + h\, m_\beta,\;\; [R_{T+h}]_{1,1} + V\bigr). \]



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Fully worked numerical example --- local-level (RW + noise), Case B, $W > 0$.}}

\emph{Parameters.} $W = \sigma_w^2 = 0.156$,\quad $V = \sigma^2 = 1$,\quad $m_0 = 1$,\quad $C_0 = 4$,\quad $y_1 = 2$,\quad $y_2 = 2.5$. $G = F = 1$ throughout.

\emph{After each numeric value, we show how to obtain it directly via $E[\cdot]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\cdot)$ on the model equations --- no formula memorisation needed.}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{At $t = 0$ --- forecast $\theta_1$ and $Y_1$ (no data yet).}}

\emph{Forecast state $\theta_1$.}
\[ a_1 \;=\; G\, m_0 \;=\; 1,\qquad R_1 \;=\; G^2\, C_0 + W \;=\; 4 + 0.156 \;=\; 4.156. \quad\Rightarrow\quad \theta_1 \mid y_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(1,\, 4.156). \]
\emph{Derivation via $E/\mathrm{Var}$.} Since $\theta_1 = \theta_0 + w_1$ with $w_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, W)$ independent of $\theta_0$:
\[ a_1 = E[\theta_1] = E[\theta_0] + E[w_1] = m_0 + 0 = 1; \qquad R_1 = \mathrm{Var}(\theta_1) = \mathrm{Var}(\theta_0) + \mathrm{Var}(w_1) = C_0 + W = 4.156. \]

\emph{Forecast observation $Y_1$.}
\[ f_1 \;=\; F\, a_1 \;=\; 1, \qquad Q_1 \;=\; F^2\, R_1 + V \;=\; 4.156 + 1 \;=\; 5.156. \quad\Rightarrow\quad Y_1 \mid y_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(1,\, 5.156). \]
\emph{Derivation.} Since $Y_1 = \theta_1 + \varepsilon_1$ with $\varepsilon_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, V)$ independent:
\[ f_1 = E[Y_1] = E[\theta_1] + E[\varepsilon_1] = a_1 = 1; \qquad Q_1 = \mathrm{Var}(Y_1) = \mathrm{Var}(\theta_1) + \mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_1) = R_1 + V = 5.156. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{At $t = 1$ --- observe $y_1 = 2$; filter $\theta_1$; forecast $\theta_2$ and $Y_2$.}}

\emph{Filter $\theta_1$.} Innovation $e_1 = y_1 - f_1 = 2 - 1 = 1$; gain $K_1 = R_1/(R_1 + V) = 4.156/5.156 \approx 0.806$.
\[ m_1 \;=\; a_1 + K_1\, e_1 \;=\; 1 + 0.806 \cdot 1 \;=\; 1.806, \qquad C_1 \;=\; (1 - K_1)\, R_1 \;\approx\; 0.806. \quad\Rightarrow\quad \theta_1 \mid y_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(1.806,\, 0.806). \]
\emph{Derivation via $E/\mathrm{Var}$ (Bayes for jointly Gaussian $(\theta_1, Y_1)$).} The joint is $(\theta_1, Y_1) \sim \mathcal{N}\!\bigl((a_1, f_1),\; (\begin{smallmatrix}R_1 & R_1 \\ R_1 & Q_1\end{smallmatrix})\bigr)$

\[ m_1 = E[\theta_1 \mid Y_1 = y_1] = a_1 + R_1 Q_1^{-1}(y_1 - f_1) = 1 + 4.156/5.156 \cdot 1 = 1.806; \]
\[ C_1 = \mathrm{Var}(\theta_1 \mid Y_1 = y_1) = R_1 - R_1 Q_1^{-1} R_1 = 4.156 - 4.156^2/5.156 \approx 0.806. \]

\textbf{The crucial covariance entry to compute:}
\[ \boxed{\; \mathrm{Cov}(\theta_t, Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;=\; \mathrm{Cov}(\theta_t,\, F_t \theta_t + v_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;=\; F_t\, \mathrm{Var}(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;=\; F_t\, R_t \quad (\text{matrix form: } R_t F_t^\top). \;} \]



\emph{Forecast $\theta_2$.}
\[ a_2 \;=\; G\, m_1 \;=\; 1.806, \qquad R_2 \;=\; C_1 + W \;=\; 0.806 + 0.156 \;=\; 0.962. \quad\Rightarrow\quad \theta_2 \mid y_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(1.806,\, 0.962). \]
\emph{Derivation.} $\theta_2 = \theta_1 + w_2$, $w_2 \perp \theta_1$ given $y_1$: $E[\theta_2 \mid y_1] = E[\theta_1 \mid y_1] = m_1$; $\mathrm{Var}(\theta_2 \mid y_1) = \mathrm{Var}(\theta_1 \mid y_1) + \mathrm{Var}(w_2) = C_1 + W$.

\emph{Forecast $Y_2$.}
\[ f_2 = F\, a_2 = 1.806, \qquad Q_2 = R_2 + V = 1.962. \quad\Rightarrow\quad Y_2 \mid y_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(1.806,\, 1.962). \]
\emph{Derivation.} $Y_2 = \theta_2 + \varepsilon_2$, $\varepsilon_2 \perp \theta_2$: $E[Y_2 \mid y_1] = E[\theta_2 \mid y_1] = a_2$; $\mathrm{Var}(Y_2 \mid y_1) = \mathrm{Var}(\theta_2 \mid y_1) + \mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_2) = R_2 + V$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{At $t = 2$ --- observe $y_2 = 2.5$; filter $\theta_2$; forecast $\theta_3$ and $Y_3$.}}

\emph{Filter $\theta_2$.} $e_2 = y_2 - f_2 = 2.5 - 1.806 = 0.694$; $K_2 = R_2/(R_2+V) = 0.962/1.962 \approx 0.490$.
\[ m_2 \;=\; a_2 + K_2\, e_2 \;\approx\; 2.146, \qquad C_2 \;=\; (1 - K_2)\, R_2 \;\approx\; 0.491. \quad\Rightarrow\quad \theta_2 \mid y_{1:2} \sim \mathcal{N}(2.146,\, 0.491). \]
\emph{Derivation.} Same Gaussian-conditioning argument as $t=1$, now with prior $\mathcal{N}(a_2, R_2)$ instead of $\mathcal{N}(a_1, R_1)$ and observation $y_2$:
\[ m_2 = a_2 + R_2 Q_2^{-1}(y_2 - f_2) = 1.806 + 0.962/1.962 \cdot 0.694 \approx 2.146; \]
\[ C_2 = R_2 - R_2 Q_2^{-1} R_2 = 0.962 - 0.962^2/1.962 \approx 0.491. \]

\emph{Forecast $\theta_3$.} $a_3 = m_2 = 2.146$; $R_3 = C_2 + W = 0.647$. \;\emph{Derivation:} $\theta_3 = \theta_2 + w_3 \Rightarrow E[\theta_3 \mid y_{1:2}] = m_2$, $\mathrm{Var}(\theta_3 \mid y_{1:2}) = C_2 + W$.

\emph{Forecast $Y_3$.} $f_3 = a_3 = 2.146$; $Q_3 = R_3 + V = 1.647$. \;\emph{Derivation:} $Y_3 = \theta_3 + \varepsilon_3 \Rightarrow E[Y_3 \mid y_{1:2}] = a_3$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y_3 \mid y_{1:2}) = R_3 + V$.


Adding them is the Bayesian honesty about uncertainty: forecast bands include both. The frequentist plug-in $Y_{T+1} \mid \hat\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\hat\theta, \sigma^2)$ keeps only the $\sigma^2$ term and produces bands that are too narrow. IT IS SO OBVIOUS THE FREQUENTIST IS WRONG, JUT BECAUSE BEING $\hat \theta$ ESTIMATED it cannot be used as a fixed point. Note frequentists fixed this by a correction for estiamtion uncertainty

In Case b 5c, there is extra uncertainty by the fact the hidden state wonders freely. notice also in a random walk the random walk can end up being +1 million or -2 millions.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Example application --- random walk $+$ noise (full forecast chain).}}

\emph{Model.} State $\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} + w_t$, $w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, W)$. Obs $Y_t = \theta_t + v_t$, $v_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, V)$. So $G = 1, F = 1$.

\emph{Filter (state posterior at time $t$).} Given $\theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_{t-1},\, C_{t-1})$:
\[ \theta_t \mid y_{1:t} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_t,\, C_t), \qquad K_t = \frac{C_{t-1} + W}{C_{t-1} + W + V}, \]
\[ m_t = m_{t-1} + K_t\,(y_t - m_{t-1}), \qquad C_t = (1 - K_t)(C_{t-1} + W). \]

\emph{1-step state forecast.}
\[ \theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(a_{t+1},\, R_{t+1}) \;=\; \mathcal{N}(m_t,\, C_t + W). \]
($G=1 \Rightarrow a_{t+1} = m_t$; one extra state shock $\Rightarrow$ variance bumped by $W$.)

\emph{$h$-step state forecast (iterate $h$ times --- mean stays put, variance accumulates $h$ shocks).}
\[ \theta_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\underbrace{m_T}_{a_{T+h}},\; \underbrace{C_T + h\, W}_{R_{T+h}}). \]

\emph{$h$-step observation forecast.}
\[ Y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\underbrace{m_T}_{f_{T+h}},\; \underbrace{C_T + h\, W + V}_{Q_{T+h}}). \]

\emph{Reading the variances.} State-forecast variance grows as $C_T + hW$ \emph{linearly in horizon} (one new state shock per step). Observation-forecast variance adds one more $V$ on top --- the fixed obs-noise contribution.

\emph{Numerical illustration (simulated, $T=40, W=0.4, V=1$).} $m_T \approx -3.33$, $C_T \approx 0.46$. State forecast variance at $h = 1, 10, 25$: $0.86,\, 4.46,\, 10.46$. Obs forecast variance: $1.86,\, 5.46,\, 11.46$.

\begin{center}
\includegraphics{IMAGE_PLACEHOLDER}
\end{center}

\emph{Plot reading.} Blue $=$ in-sample filtered posterior $\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}$ with its 95\% band (tight, since data anchors $\theta_t$ each step). Red dashed $=$ forecast mean $m_T$ (flat, since $G=1$). Red darker band $=$ 95\% for $\theta_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T}$, growing as $\sqrt{C_T + hW}$ (linear in $h$ for variance, $\sqrt{h}$ for the half-width). Red lighter band $=$ 95\% for $Y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T}$, slightly wider by adding $V$.

nodes.title: Bayesian point estimation: loss functions and the posterior mean
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{BAYESIAN POINT ESTIMATION --- summary measures from a posterior via expected loss.}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{When this comes up.}} \emph{Post-processing step after Bayesian inference.} You first run whatever Bayesian computation gives you a posterior --- filter for $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})$, Bayes' rule for $f(\theta \mid y)$, MCMC samples, etc. \emph{Then}, maybe you want to report a single number summary $\hat a$ rather than the whole distribution.
In linear-Gaussian DLMs the Kalman filter already returns this number ($m_t$) for free --- so you rarely think about the decision rule, but it is implicitly squared loss.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bayes estimator (general formula).}}
L = loss fucntion
\[ \boxed{\; \hat a^* \;=\; \arg\min_{a}\, E\bigl[L(\theta, a) \mid y\bigr] \;=\; \arg\min_{a}\, \int L(\theta, a)\, f(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta. \;} \]
\emph{loss $\times$ posterior weight}, integrated over $\theta$ (we don't know $\theta$, we only have its posterior distribution).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Three classic loss functions and their Bayes estimators.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{Squared loss} $L(\theta, a) = (\theta - a)^2$ $\;\Rightarrow\;$ $\hat a^* = E[\theta \mid y]$ (\emph{posterior mean}).

$\bullet$ \textbf{Absolute loss} $L(\theta, a) = |\theta - a|$ $\;\Rightarrow\;$ $\hat a^* = \mathrm{median}(\theta \mid y)$ (\emph{posterior median}).

$\bullet$ \textbf{0--1 loss} $L(\theta, a) = \mathbf{1}\{\theta \neq a\}$ $\;\Rightarrow\;$ $\hat a^* = \arg\max_\theta f(\theta \mid y)$ (\emph{posterior mode = MAP}).

$\bullet$ \textbf{Asymmetric loss} (e.g.\ $\alpha (\theta - a)_+ + \beta (a - \theta)_+$) $\;\Rightarrow\;$ a \emph{posterior quantile}. Common in finance / inventory / energy where over- vs.\ under-prediction cost differently.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why squared loss gives the posterior mean (1-line proof).}}
\[ E[(\theta - a)^2 \mid y] \;=\; E[\theta^2 \mid y] - 2 a\, E[\theta \mid y] + a^2. \]
Differentiate with respect to $a$ and set to zero: $-2 E[\theta \mid y] + 2 a = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \hat a^* = E[\theta \mid y]$. (Second derivative $= 2 > 0$: it is a minimum.)

nodes.title: Example 2: Trend DLMs: global, RW+drift, LLT / Local linear growth, DLR (one note)
Proof analytic marginals recursion
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof of the analytical-marginal formulas (RTS).}}

\emph{(i) Marginalisation + chain rule.}
\[ \pi(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T})  \; \underbrace{=}_{\text{ Marginalisation + chain rule}}\; \int \underbrace{\pi(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1},\, y_{1:T})}_{\pi(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1},\, y_{1:t}) \text{ by (1)}} \, \pi(\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:T})\, d\theta_{t+1} \]
(1) Given $\theta_{t+1}$, the future observations $y_{t+1:T}$ add no information about $\theta_t$


\emph{(ii) Compute the backward kernel $\pi(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1}, y_{1:t})$ via Bayes (likelihood $\times$ prior):} 
\[ \pi(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1},\, y_{1:t}) \;\propto\; \overbrace{\pi(\theta_{t+1} \mid \theta_t,\, y_{1:t})}^{\text{likelihood, simplify:} \pi(\theta_{t+1} \mid \theta_t)}\, \overbrace{\pi(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})}^{\text{prior}} \]

 Both factors are Gaussian (read off the filter and the model):
- From the state equation gaussiani + $G_{t+1}\theta_t$ fixed once you now $\theta_t$. \[ \pi(\theta_{t+1} \mid \theta_t) = \mathcal{N}(G_{t+1}\theta_t,\, W_{t+1})\]
- This you already know: 
\[\pi(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) = \mathcal{N}(m_t, C_t). \]
Note how you would have an expected value as mean instead. 

(iii) By Gaussian conditionting, with $J_t = C_t\, G_{t+1}^\top\, R_{t+1}^{-1}$:
\[ \theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1},\, y_{1:t} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\, m_t + J_t(\theta_{t+1} - a_{t+1}),\;\; C_t - J_t\, G_{t+1}\, C_t \,\bigr). \]

\emph{(iv) Take expectation and variance of the integral (tower rules).}

\emph{Mean.} $\;s_t = E[\theta_t \mid y_{1:T}] = E\bigl[E[\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1}, y_{1:t}] \mid y_{1:T}\bigr] = E\bigl[m_t + J_t(\theta_{t+1} - a_{t+1}) \mid y_{1:T}\bigr]$
\[ \;=\; m_t + J_t\, (s_{t+1} - a_{t+1}), \]
using $E[\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:T}] = s_{t+1}$. \quad $\checkmark$

\emph{Variance.} Law of total variance:
\[ S_t \;=\; E\bigl[\mathrm{Var}(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1}, y_{1:t}) \mid y_{1:T}\bigr] + \mathrm{Var}\bigl(E[\theta_t \mid \theta_{t+1}, y_{1:t}] \mid y_{1:T}\bigr). \]
The first term is constant (the conditional variance doesn't depend on $\theta_{t+1}$): $C_t - J_t G_{t+1} C_t$. The second is $\mathrm{Var}(J_t \theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:T}) = J_t S_{t+1} J_t^\top$. So
\[ S_t \;=\; C_t - J_t\, G_{t+1}\, C_t + J_t\, S_{t+1}\, J_t^\top. \]
Use $J_t G_{t+1} C_t = J_t R_{t+1} J_t^\top$ (since $J_t = C_t G_{t+1}^\top R_{t+1}^{-1}$ $\Rightarrow$ $J_t R_{t+1} = C_t G_{t+1}^\top$ $\Rightarrow$ $J_t R_{t+1} J_t^\top = C_t G_{t+1}^\top J_t^\top = J_t G_{t+1} C_t$) to rewrite:
\[ S_t \;=\; C_t - J_t\, (R_{t+1} - S_{t+1})\, J_t^\top. \quad \checkmark \]

nodes.title: Fixed regression model (cross-sectional, no time)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FIXED REGRESSION MODEL (cross-sectional, no time dimension; per-observation slope $\beta_i$).}}

Regression of $Y$ on a covariate $x$ across \emph{individuals} (index $i$, not time). Slope $\beta_i$ is allowed to vary per observation.

\begin{keydef}
\textbf{Cross-sectional regression with individual-specific slope.}
\[ Y_i \;=\; \alpha + \beta_i\, x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma^2), \qquad i = 1, \dots, n. \]
$\alpha$ is the common intercept; $\beta_i$ is the slope for observation $i$ (can differ across $i$); $\sigma^2$ is the noise variance. Index $i$ runs over individuals/observations, \emph{not} time.
\end{keydef}

\emph{Identifiability caveat.} With $n$ observations and $n$ unknown slopes, the model is \emph{not identified} without further structure on $\beta_i$. Four standard restrictions, all of which collapse the model back into a single DLM with a static state and a richer $F_i$:

$\bullet$ \emph{Case A --- $\beta_i$ depends on a known covariate $z_i$ (interaction).}
\[ \beta_i = \beta_0 + \gamma\, z_i \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; Y_i = \alpha + \beta_0 x_i + \gamma (z_i x_i) + \varepsilon_i. \]
Effect of $x$ depends linearly on $z$ (e.g., $z =$ age $\Rightarrow$ price elasticity varies with age).

$\bullet$ \emph{Case B --- $\beta_i$ depends on $x_i$ itself (polynomial / non-linear effect).}
\[ \beta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; Y_i = \alpha + \beta_0 x_i + \beta_1 x_i^2 + \varepsilon_i \quad (\text{quadratic regression}). \]
Slope changes with the level of $x_i$ (diminishing returns if $\beta_1 < 0$).

$\bullet$ \emph{Case C --- $\beta_i$ is group-specific (categorical) --- $K$ slopes total.}
\[ Y_i = \alpha + \beta_{g(i)}\, x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad g(i) \in \{1, \dots, K\}. \]
Each group has its own slope; estimated by interaction dummies $\mathbf{1}\{g(i) = k\}\, x_i$ for each group.

$\bullet$ \emph{Case D --- $\beta_i$ is a random effect (hierarchical model).}
\[ \beta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar\beta,\, \tau^2), \quad Y_i \mid \beta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\alpha + \beta_i x_i,\, \sigma^2). \]
$\beta_i$ are unobserved random draws from a population; estimate $(\bar\beta, \tau^2)$ rather than each $\beta_i$ separately. Posterior gives a \emph{shrunken} $\hat\beta_i$ pulled toward $\bar\beta$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Conditional distribution per $x_i$.}}
\[ Y_i \mid x_i \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\alpha + \beta_i\, x_i,\; \sigma^2). \]
At each $x_i$ value, the conditional density is Gaussian centered on $\alpha + \beta_i x_i$, width $\sigma$. The plot below visualises this for the homogeneous-slope special case ($\beta_i \equiv \beta$ constant), showing how the conditional mean shifts with $x_i$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4-step DLM template (degenerate, static state).}}

\emph{(1) State.} $\theta = (\alpha, \beta_0, \dots)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^k$, \emph{frozen} (no time index, no dynamics). The components of $\theta$ are whatever parameters define $\beta_i$ in the case above (Case A: $(\alpha, \beta_0, \gamma)$; Case B: $(\alpha, \beta_0, \beta_1)$; Case C: $(\alpha, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_K)$; Case D: $(\alpha, \bar\beta, \tau^2, \sigma^2)$ at top of a hierarchy).

\emph{(2) Component equations.} All components frozen: $\theta_{j} = \theta_{j}$. No noise.

\emph{(3) Matrix state eq.} $\theta_i = G\, \theta_{i-1} + w_i = I_k \theta_{i-1} + 0 = \theta_{i-1}$ (state never changes across $i$). $G = I_k$, $W = 0$.

\emph{(4) Observation eq.} $Y_i = F_i\, \theta + \varepsilon_i$ with a \emph{case-dependent} $F_i$:
\[ \text{Case A: } F_i = (1, x_i, z_i x_i); \quad \text{Case B: } F_i = (1, x_i, x_i^2); \quad \text{Case C: } F_i = (1, \mathbf{1}\{g(i)=1\}x_i, \dots, \mathbf{1}\{g(i)=K\}x_i); \]
\[ \text{Case D: } F_i = (1, x_i) \text{ plus latent } \beta_i \text{ in the state (hierarchical SSM)}. \]
$\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Vs.\ Dynamic Linear Regression (DLR, Example 7).}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Fixed regression (this):} coefficients vary \emph{across individuals} $i$ but not across time; state frozen.

$\bullet$ \emph{DLR:} coefficients vary \emph{over time} $t$ (random walks); state evolves; same $F_t = (1, x_t)$ shape.

\emph{Bridge.} DLR is the time-domain analog of Case D of fixed regression: $\beta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar\beta, \tau^2)$ iid across individuals becomes $\beta_t$ random walk across time. Both relax "$\beta$ same everywhere" along different axes (cross-section vs time).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Estimation.}} Cases A--C are standard OLS / MLE: stack the appropriate columns of $F_i$ as a design matrix and regress. Case D needs hierarchical Bayes / mixed-effects (\verb|lmer| in R, \verb|brms| or \verb|stan|).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why include this in the SSM family map?}} The most degenerate DLM: no time, no dynamics, no state noise --- just a static parameter vector with a per-observation observation matrix $F_i$. Serves as the \emph{baseline} that the dynamic models (LLT / Local linear growth, DLR, etc.) generalise. Plot below visualises the conditional distribution that defines this model.

nodes.title: VAR (Vector AutoRegression) as state-space model
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{VECTOR AUTOREGRESSION (VAR) AS STATE-SPACE MODEL.}}

Multivariate extension of AR: each component depends on lagged values of \emph{every} component (its own and the others'). Captures \emph{joint dynamics} (Granger causality, impulse-response analysis).

\emph{Footnote --- book status.} Petris (\S3.3.7, p.\ 141) explicitly notes ``\emph{we will not treat VAR models or cointegration in this book}'' --- VAR is mentioned only as a special case of multivariate ARMA (eq.\ 3.50, no MA part). The DLM below is the natural specialization of that ARMA-DLM with $q = 0, p = 1$: state $=$ current vector, $G = \Phi$, $F = I$, $V = 0$. Standard treatment in econometrics texts (L\"utkepohl 2005, Canova 2007).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{VAR(1) on two series $X, Y$ --- 4-step DLM template.}}

\emph{(1) State (with components).} $\theta_t = (X_t,\, Y_t)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^2$, where $X_t$ and $Y_t$ are the two observed series at time $t$.

\emph{(2) Component equations.}
\[ X_t \;=\; \phi_{11}\, X_{t-1} + \phi_{12}\, Y_{t-1} + w_{1,t}, \]
\[ Y_t \;=\; \phi_{21}\, X_{t-1} + \phi_{22}\, Y_{t-1} + w_{2,t}, \]
with $(w_{1,t},\, w_{2,t})^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_2(0,\, \Sigma)$, $\Sigma = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma_1^2 & \sigma_{12} \\ \sigma_{12} & \sigma_2^2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.

\emph{Reading.} Each line shows: $X_t$ depends on $X_{t-1}$ AND $Y_{t-1}$ (own lag $+$ cross-lag); symmetrically for $Y_t$. Off-diagonal $\phi_{12}, \phi_{21}$ encode the cross-influence; $\sigma_{12}$ encodes contemporaneous correlation in the shocks.

\emph{(3) Matrix state equation.}
\[ \theta_t \;=\; G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix}\phi_{11} & \phi_{12} \\ \phi_{21} & \phi_{22}\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}X_{t-1} \\ Y_{t-1}\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}w_{1,t} \\ w_{2,t}\end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix}\phi_{11} X_{t-1} + \phi_{12} Y_{t-1} + w_{1,t} \\ \phi_{21} X_{t-1} + \phi_{22} Y_{t-1} + w_{2,t}\end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix}X_t \\ Y_t\end{pmatrix}. \]
$G = \Phi = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\phi_{11} & \phi_{12} \\ \phi_{21} & \phi_{22}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, $W = \Sigma$.

\emph{Distributional form.} $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_2\!\bigl(\Phi\, \theta_{t-1},\; \Sigma\bigr)$.

\emph{(4) Observation equation.} The state IS the observation (VAR is directly observed):
\[ \mathbf{Y}_t \;=\; (X_t,\, Y_t)^\top =  F\, \theta_t + v_t \;=\; I_2\, \theta_t + 0 \;=\; \theta_t \]
with $F = I_2$, $V = 0$ (degenerate DLM --- like AR but multivariate).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why VAR matters.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Multivariate dependence.} Each component depends not only on its own lags but on every other component's lags. Captures Granger causality, impulse responses, dynamic interactions.

$\bullet$ \emph{Workhorse of macroeconometrics.} Sims (1980) introduced VAR for empirical macro --- modelling joint dynamics of GDP, inflation, interest rates, etc.

$\bullet$ \emph{Filtering / forecasting via Kalman.} Once in DLM form, all the usual machinery applies: filter for state, forecast at horizon $h$, MLE on $(\Phi, \Sigma)$ via the prediction-error decomposition.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Connections.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{$q = 1$:} VAR collapses to AR(1) --- single scalar series.

$\bullet$ \emph{Adding measurement noise} ($V > 0$): "VAR + noise" or dynamic factor model (DFM) structure; common in finance for latent factors driving observed prices.

$\bullet$ \emph{HMM analog:} discrete-state version is multi-state HMM with state-dependent emissions.

nodes.title: SUTSE (Seemingly Unrelated Time Series) as state-space model
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SEEMINGLY UNRELATED TIME SERIES EQUATIONS (SUTSE) --- Petris \S3.3.2, p.\ 127.}}


SUTSE = stack $m$ LLTs (each piece has latent level + slope, driven internally)   

Stack $m$ structural univariate DLMs (each series has its OWN level + slope --- a Local Linear Trend), then let the \emph{state-noise shocks correlate across series}. 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SUTSE on two series $X, Y$ (each Local Linear Trend) --- 4-step DLM template.}}

\emph{(1) State (with components).} $\theta_t = (\mu_t^X,\, \mu_t^Y,\, \beta_t^X,\, \beta_t^Y)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^4$, where $\mu_t^{X}, \mu_t^{Y}$ are the (latent) \emph{levels} of the two series and $\beta_t^{X}, \beta_t^{Y}$ are their \emph{slopes}. Book convention: group by component (all levels first, then all slopes).

\emph{Footnote --- equivalent matrix form.} You can organize the same state as a $2 \times 2$ \emph{matrix} $\Theta_t = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\mu_t^X & \beta_t^X \\ \mu_t^Y & \beta_t^Y\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$. The first column is component vector 

\emph{(2) Component equations (each series is its own LLT).}
\[ \mu_t^X = \mu_{t-1}^X + \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{1,t}, \qquad \mu_t^Y = \mu_{t-1}^Y + \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{2,t}, \]
\[ \beta_t^X = \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{3,t}, \qquad \beta_t^Y = \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{4,t}, \]
with $(w_{1,t}, w_{2,t}, w_{3,t}, w_{4,t})^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_4(0,\, W)$ and \emph{block-diagonal}
\[ W = \begin{pmatrix} W_\mu & 0 \\ 0 & W_\beta \end{pmatrix}, \quad W_\mu = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{\mu_X}^2 & \sigma_{\mu_{XY}} \\ \sigma_{\mu_{XY}} & \sigma_{\mu_Y}^2\end{pmatrix}, \quad W_\beta = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{\beta_X}^2 & \sigma_{\beta_{XY}} \\ \sigma_{\beta_{XY}} & \sigma_{\beta_Y}^2\end{pmatrix}. \]

\emph{Reading.} $\mu_t^X$ depends \textbf{only} on its own past $(\mu_{t-1}^X, \beta_{t-1}^X)$, never on $\mu_{t-1}^Y$. Same for the others --- \emph{no cross-coupling in the dynamics}. The cross-series link lives in the off-diagonals $\sigma_{\mu_{XY}}$ and $\sigma_{\beta_{XY}}$: shocks to the two levels (and to the two slopes) are contemporaneously correlated.

\emph{(3) Matrix state equation.}
\[ \theta_t \;=\; G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mu_{t-1}^X \\ \mu_{t-1}^Y \\ \beta_{t-1}^X \\ \beta_{t-1}^Y \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} w_{1,t} \\ w_{2,t} \\ w_{3,t} \\ w_{4,t} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \mu_{t-1}^X + \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{1,t} \\ \mu_{t-1}^Y + \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{2,t} \\ \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{3,t} \\ \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{4,t} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \mu_t^X \\ \mu_t^Y \\ \beta_t^X \\ \beta_t^Y \end{pmatrix}. \]
Equivalently $G = G_{\mathrm{LLT}} \otimes I_2$ with $G_{\mathrm{LLT}} = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ (Kronecker form, book eq.\ 3.40).

\emph{Distributional form.} $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_4\!\bigl(G\, \theta_{t-1},\; W\bigr)$, with $W = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\mu, W_\beta)$ as above.

\emph{(4) Observation equation (only the levels are observed).}
\[ Y_t = \begin{pmatrix} X_t \\ Y_t \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{F} \theta_t + \begin{pmatrix} v_{1,t} \\ v_{2,t} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix} v_{1,t} \\ v_{2,t} \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}_2(0,\, V), \]
with $V$ a $2 \times 2$ matrix (book allows $V$ non-diagonal, adding a \emph{further} cross-series link in obs noise on top of the main one in $W$).

\emph{Multiplying out $F\, \theta_t$:}
\[ F\, \theta_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \mu_t^X \\ \mu_t^Y \end{pmatrix} \;\Longrightarrow\; \begin{pmatrix} X_t \\ Y_t \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \mu_t^X + v_{1,t} \\ \mu_t^Y + v_{2,t} \end{pmatrix}. \]

\emph{Distributional form.} $\bigl(X_t, Y_t\bigr)^\top \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}_2\!\bigl(F\, \theta_t,\; V\bigr)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Contrast with VAR.}}

\begin{tabular}{l|l|l}
& \textbf{VAR(1)} & \textbf{SUTSE} \\
\hline
\emph{State} & $(X_t, Y_t)$ directly & $(\mu_t^X, \mu_t^Y, \beta_t^X, \beta_t^Y)$ (latent) \\
\emph{Transition $G$} & dense ($\phi_{12}, \phi_{21} \ne 0$) & block, no cross-series coupling \\
\emph{Source of link} & lagged cross-effects in $G$ & shock correlation in $W$ \\
\emph{Granger causality} & possible & no (no lagged-$X$ effect on $Y$) \\
\emph{Observation $F$} & $I_2$ (state $=$ obs) & picks out levels only \\
\end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why SUTSE is useful.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Efficiency gain over separate equations.} If you fit each series on its own (ignoring the cross-series covariances), estimates are still consistent but lose efficiency. Using the joint covariance gives smaller standard errors --- Zellner's classic SUR result (1962).

$\bullet$ \emph{Common shocks.} The off-diagonals in $W_\mu, W_\beta$ capture \emph{shared exposure to a common factor} (oil price shock affecting both GDP and inflation; market-wide shock to two stocks).

$\bullet$ \emph{Sparser than VAR.} If you believe the series are dynamically independent but driven by common shocks, SUTSE uses fewer parameters --- no off-diagonal entries in $G$, only correlations in the noise.




\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Special cases.}}

$\bullet$ $W_\mu, W_\beta$ both diagonal and $V$ diagonal: SUTSE collapses to \emph{two independent univariate LLTs} --- can be fit separately.

$\bullet$ $W_\mu = 0$: levels follow integrated random walks (slopes drift, levels accumulate). Common simplification.

$\bullet$ $m = 1$: collapses to a single Local Linear Trend (Example 5).

$\bullet$ All slopes $\beta_t^{X} = \beta_t^{Y} = 0$ and $W_\beta = 0$: collapses to two correlated random walks (no trend), with link via $W_\mu$.

nodes.title: SUR (dynamic, multivariate) as state-space model
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SEEMINGLY UNRELATED REGRESSIONS (SUR), DYNAMIC --- Petris \S3.3.3, p.\ 132.}}

now you have m assets = m time series $y_i$

SUR = stack $m$ DLRs (each piece is a regression on an external $x_t$), then let the noise covariances correlate across equations. 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SUR on two series $X, Y$ with common regressor $x_t$ --- 4-step DLM template.}}

\emph{(1) State (with components --- book convention: group by component type).} $\theta_t = (\alpha_t^X,\, \alpha_t^Y,\, \beta_t^X,\, \beta_t^Y)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^4$, where $\alpha_t^X, \alpha_t^Y$ are the (drifting) \emph{intercepts} of the two equations and $\beta_t^X, \beta_t^Y$ are the (drifting) \emph{slopes} on the common regressor $x_t$.

\emph{(2) Component equations (each coefficient is a random walk).}
\[ \alpha_t^X = \alpha_{t-1}^X + w_{1,t}, \qquad \alpha_t^Y = \alpha_{t-1}^Y + w_{2,t}, \]
\[ \beta_t^X = \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{3,t}, \qquad \beta_t^Y = \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{4,t}, \]
note here we keep the slope seprate form the intercept, this is a conceptual point, we could have put them together, but the idea is that alfa and beta are decsribign two very different things
with $(w_{1,t}, w_{2,t}, w_{3,t}, w_{4,t})^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_4(0,\, W)$ and \emph{block-diagonal}
\[ W = \begin{pmatrix} W_\alpha & 0 \\ 0 & W_\beta \end{pmatrix}, \quad W_\alpha = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{\alpha_X}^2 & \sigma_{\alpha_{XY}} \\ \sigma_{\alpha_{XY}} & \sigma_{\alpha_Y}^2\end{pmatrix}, \quad W_\beta = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{\beta_X}^2 & \sigma_{\beta_{XY}} \\ \sigma_{\beta_{XY}} & \sigma_{\beta_Y}^2\end{pmatrix}. \]
\emph{Primary SUR link in state noise:} off-diagonals $\sigma_{\alpha_{XY}}, \sigma_{\beta_{XY}}$ couple the intercept shocks across series and the slope shocks across series.

\emph{(3) Matrix state equation.}
\[ \theta_t \;=\; G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t \;=\; I_4 \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_{t-1}^X \\ \alpha_{t-1}^Y \\ \beta_{t-1}^X \\ \beta_{t-1}^Y \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} w_{1,t} \\ w_{2,t} \\ w_{3,t} \\ w_{4,t} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_{t-1}^X + w_{1,t} \\ \alpha_{t-1}^Y + w_{2,t} \\ \beta_{t-1}^X + w_{3,t} \\ \beta_{t-1}^Y + w_{4,t} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_t^X \\ \alpha_t^Y \\ \beta_t^X \\ \beta_t^Y \end{pmatrix}. \]
$G = I_4$ (coefficients evolve independently in mean), all cross-series coupling pushed into $W$.

\emph{Distributional form.} $\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_4\!\bigl(\theta_{t-1},\; W\bigr)$, with $W = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\alpha, W_\beta)$ as above.

\emph{(4) Observation equation (Kronecker form, book eq.\ 3.42).}
\[ Y_t = \begin{pmatrix} X_t \\ Y_t \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & x_t & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & x_t \end{pmatrix}}_{F_t \;=\; (1,\,x_t) \,\otimes\, I_2} \theta_t + \begin{pmatrix} v_{1,t} \\ v_{2,t} \end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{pmatrix} v_{1,t} \\ v_{2,t} \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}_2(0,\, V), \]
with $V = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\sigma_{v_X}^2 & \sigma_{v_{XY}} \\ \sigma_{v_{XY}} & \sigma_{v_Y}^2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ also possibly non-diagonal (secondary cross-series link).

\emph{Multiplying out $F_t\, \theta_t$:}
\[ F_t\, \theta_t = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_t^X + \beta_t^X\, x_t \\ \alpha_t^Y + \beta_t^Y\, x_t \end{pmatrix} \;\Longrightarrow\; \begin{pmatrix} X_t \\ Y_t \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_t^X + \beta_t^X\, x_t + v_{1,t} \\ \alpha_t^Y + \beta_t^Y\, x_t + v_{2,t} \end{pmatrix}. \]

\emph{Distributional form.} $\bigl(X_t, Y_t\bigr)^\top \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}_2\!\bigl(F_t\, \theta_t,\; V\bigr)$.
Both equations use the SAME regressor $x_t$ but with their own (drifting) intercept and slope --- "seemingly unrelated" because they appear independent yet are linked through correlated noises.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{General $m$-asset SUR --- compact Kronecker form.}}

For $m$ response series $Y_t^{(1)}, \dots, Y_t^{(m)}$ regressed on a common scalar $x_t$:

\emph{(1) State.} $\theta_t = \bigl(\alpha_t^{(1)}, \dots, \alpha_t^{(m)},\, \beta_t^{(1)}, \dots, \beta_t^{(m)}\bigr)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{2m}$.

\emph{(2) Component equations.} For each $i = 1, \dots, m$:
\[ \alpha_t^{(i)} = \alpha_{t-1}^{(i)} + w_{\alpha,t}^{(i)}, \qquad \beta_t^{(i)} = \beta_{t-1}^{(i)} + w_{\beta,t}^{(i)}, \]
\[ \bigl(w_{\alpha,t}^{(1)}, \dots, w_{\alpha,t}^{(m)},\, w_{\beta,t}^{(1)}, \dots, w_{\beta,t}^{(m)}\bigr)^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_{2m}(0,\, W), \quad W = \mathrm{blkdiag}(W_\alpha, W_\beta), \]
with $W_\alpha, W_\beta$ each $m \times m$ (typically non-diagonal --- the primary cross-asset link).

\emph{(3) Matrix state equation.} $G = I_{2m}$, so
\[ \theta_t = G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad \theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}_{2m}(\theta_{t-1},\, W). \]

\emph{(4) Observation equation.} $F_t = (1, x_t) \otimes I_m$, an $m \times 2m$ matrix:
\[ \mathbf{Y}_t = F_t\, \theta_t + v_t, \qquad v_t \sim \mathcal{N}_m(0,\, V), \]
with $\mathbf{Y}_t = (Y_t^{(1)}, \dots, Y_t^{(m)})^\top$ and $V$ an $m \times m$ (possibly non-diagonal) matrix. Component-wise:
\[ Y_t^{(i)} = \alpha_t^{(i)} + \beta_t^{(i)}\, x_t + v_t^{(i)}, \quad i = 1, \dots, m. \]
\emph{Distributional form.} $\mathbf{Y}_t \mid \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}_m\!\bigl(F_t\, \theta_t,\, V\bigr)$.

\emph{Parameter counts.} State noise: $m(m+1)$ free entries in $W_\alpha + W_\beta$. Obs noise: $m(m+1)/2$ in $V$. So total $\mathcal{O}(m^2)$ noise parameters --- scales gracefully with $m$ thanks to the Kronecker structure.

\emph{CAPM example.} $m = 4$ assets (Mobil, IBM, Weyer, Citicorp), $x_t = R_{m,t} - R_{f,t}$ shared market excess return. State $\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}^8$ (4 alphas $+$ 4 betas); $W_\alpha, W_\beta$ are $4 \times 4$; $V$ is $4 \times 4$ (cross-stock residual correlation).

nodes.title: Model checking: forecast errors / innovations
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MODEL CHECKING --- forecast errors / innovations.}}

Once a DLM is fit (filter run, parameters estimated), check whether the model is adequate by inspecting the one-step-ahead \emph{forecast errors} (a.k.a.\ \emph{innovations / residuals}).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Forecast error and one-step decomposition.}}

\emph{One-step forecast (Kalman):} $f_t = \mathbb{E}(Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$.

\emph{One-step forecast variance:} $Q_t = \mathrm{Var}(Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$.

\emph{Forecast error / innovation / residual:}
\[ \boxed{\; e_t \;=\; y_t - f_t \;=\; y_t - \mathbb{E}(Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;} \]
So we can decompose every observation as
\[ y_t \;=\; \underbrace{f_t}_{\text{forecast (known at }t-1)} \;+\; \underbrace{e_t}_{\text{innovation: the new info at }t}. \]
$f_t$ is what the model expected before seeing $y_t$; $e_t$ is the surprise.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{What well-specified residuals should look like.}}

If the model is correct, the innovations $\{e_t\}$ are \emph{independent across time} (they extract all serial information; nothing predictable left) and Gaussian:
\[ e_t \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(0,\, Q_t) \quad\text{independently across }t. \]
\emph{Standardised innovations:}
\[ \tilde e_t \;=\; \frac{e_t}{\sqrt{Q_t}} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(0,\, 1) \quad\text{i.i.d.} \]
This is the object you actually plot / test. Checks:

$\bullet$ \emph{Normality:} Q--Q plot of $\{\tilde e_t\}$ against $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$; Shapiro--Wilk.

$\bullet$ \emph{No autocorrelation:} ACF/PACF of $\{\tilde e_t\}$ should look like white noise; Ljung--Box test.

$\bullet$ \emph{Variance stable:} time plot of $\tilde e_t$ --- no heteroskedasticity / outliers / change-points.

If any of these fails, the model is mis-specified (wrong $G, F, V, W$, missing component, wrong noise distribution, $\dots$).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Exercise (Petris Prop.\ 2.7, p.\ 73) --- the standardised innovations are iid $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.}}

\emph{Claim.} Under a correctly specified DLM, the sequence $\{\tilde e_t\} = \{e_t / \sqrt{Q_t}\}$ is a Gaussian white noise: iid $\mathcal{N}(0,\, 1)$.

The proof has four pieces. The key technical tool is the \emph{Law of Iterated Expectations (LIE)}: $\mathbb{E}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}(X \mid \mathcal{F})]$ for any sigma-algebra $\mathcal{F}$.

\emph{(i) Zero mean: $\mathbb{E}(e_t) = 0$.}

\[ \mathbb{E}(e_t) \;=\; \mathbb{E}(Y_t - f_t) \;\overset{\text{LIE}}{=}\; \mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\, \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\bigl(Y_t - f_t \mid y_{1:t-1}\bigr)}_{\text{condition on past}}\,\bigr] \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\, \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{=\, f_t \text{ by definition}} \;-\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(f_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{=\, f_t,\text{ see below}}\,\bigr] \;=\; \mathbb{E}[\, f_t - f_t\,] \;=\; 0. \]

\emph{Why $\mathbb{E}(f_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) = f_t$?} Because $f_t = \mathbb{E}(Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$ is by construction a \emph{function of} $y_{1:t-1}$ (computed by the Kalman filter from data up to $t-1$). A random variable that is already determined by the conditioning sigma-algebra equals its own conditional expectation --- conditioning on what you already know doesn't change it.

\emph{(ii) Uncorrelated across time: $\mathrm{Cov}(e_t, e_s) = 0$ for $s < t$.}

\emph{Why $e_s$ is past-measurable.} For $s < t$, $e_s = Y_s - f_s$ is a function of $Y_{1:s}$ (since $f_s$ is computed by the Kalman filter from $y_{1:s-1}$). Because $s < t$, we have $\{Y_1, \dots, Y_s\} \subseteq \{Y_1, \dots, Y_{t-1}\}$, so $e_s$ is also a function of $y_{1:t-1}$. Call it
\[ e_s \;=\; g(y_{1:t-1}) \;=:\; Z. \]
So $Z$ is past-measurable (known once you condition on $y_{1:t-1}$).

\emph{Apply LIE.}
\[ \mathrm{Cov}(e_t, e_s) \;=\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(e_t\, Z)}_{\mathrm{Cov} \,-\, \mathbb{E}(e_t)\mathbb{E}(Z),\ \mathbb{E}(e_t) = 0 \text{ by (i)}} \;\overset{\text{LIE}}{=}\; \mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\, \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(e_t\, Z \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{Z \text{ pulls out, past-meas.}}\,\bigr] \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\, Z \cdot \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(e_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{=\, 0 \text{ as in (i)}}\,\bigr] \;=\; 0. \]
Z can be pulled out, recall it is $y_t - f_t$, so for that conditioning it is fully detemrined

\emph{(iii) Variance --- needs the \emph{law of total variance} (LTV).} For any random variable $X$ and sigma-algebra $\mathcal{F}$:
\[ \mathrm{Var}(X) \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\mathrm{Var}(X \mid \mathcal{F})\bigr] \;+\; \mathrm{Var}\!\bigl[\mathbb{E}(X \mid \mathcal{F})\bigr]. \]
Apply with $X = e_t$, $\mathcal{F} = y_{1:t-1}$:
\[ \mathrm{Var}(e_t) \;\overset{\text{LTV}}{=}\; \mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\, \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}(e_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{=\, Q_t,\ \text{see below}}\,\bigr] \;+\; \mathrm{Var}\!\bigl[\, \underbrace{\mathbb{E}(e_t \mid y_{1:t-1})}_{=\, 0 \text{ as in (i)}}\,\bigr] \;=\; \mathbb{E}[Q_t] \;+\; \mathrm{Var}[0] \;=\; \mathbb{E}[Q_t]. \]

\emph{Why $\mathrm{Var}(e_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) = Q_t$?}
\[ \mathrm{Var}(e_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;=\; \mathrm{Var}(Y_t - f_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;\overset{(\star)}{=}\; \mathrm{Var}(Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;=\; Q_t. \]
$(\star)$: $f_t$ is a constant given that conditioning.

\emph{(iv) Put it all together --- standardise.}

\emph{Conditional law.} In a Gaussian DLM, the Kalman filter gives $Y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(f_t,\, Q_t)$. Subtract the constant $f_t$ (past-measurable):
\[ e_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(0,\, Q_t). \]
\emph{Standardise.} $Q_t$ is past-measurable $\Rightarrow$ a constant under $\mathbb{E}(\cdot \mid y_{1:t-1})$. Divide $e_t$ by $\sqrt{Q_t}$:
\[ \tilde e_t \;=\; \frac{e_t}{\sqrt{Q_t}} \;\Bigm|\; y_{1:t-1} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(0,\, 1). \]
\emph{Marginalise.} This conditional law does \emph{not depend on} $y_{1:t-1}$, so the marginal is the same: $\tilde e_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$. Idea: if $X \mid Y$ has the same distribution for every $Y$, then $X$ is independent of $Y$, and     marginally $X$ just has that distribution. The conditioning is doing no work.

\emph{Independence.} The whole $\{e_t\}$ process is jointly Gaussian (linear combinations of jointly Gaussian $Y$'s), and by (ii) they are pairwise uncorrelated. For jointly Gaussian variables, uncorrelated $\Leftrightarrow$ independent. Standardising preserves this.

\emph{Conclusion.} $\{\tilde e_t\}$ is iid $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. $\square$

trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{TIME-SERIES INFERENCE --- PRINT-READY DOSSIER}}

\emph{Self-contained merge of nine snippets covering the SSM inference toolkit, ordered from the basic Bayesian recursion (filtering) through observation prediction, smoothing and decoding, the Gaussian closed form, and two end-to-end worked examples. Page references in the worked examples are to Petris--Petrone--Campagnoli (DLMwR).}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Table of contents.}}
$\bullet$ 1. Filtering
$\bullet$ 2. State Prediction
$\bullet$ 3. Observation Prediction
$\bullet$ 4. Smoothing and Decoding
$\bullet$ 5. Decoding --- Viterbi detail
$\bullet$ 6. Gaussian Simplification (closed-form predictive)
$\bullet$ 7. Posterior Mean and Precision (algebraic form)
$\bullet$ 8. Worked Example 1 --- RW + noise, fixed state
$\bullet$ 9. Worked Example 2 --- RW + noise, dynamic state ($W > 0$)

================================================================================

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Filtering}}


NOW WE USE BAYES RULE: 


Recall: $y_{1:T}$ is it like $P(y_1, y_2, ... y_T)$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Filtering (state estimation)} $\;\;f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})$.} \emph{What is the state today, given everything observed up to today?}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Generic Bayes with background --- the only formula we use.}}
\[ \boxed{\; f(A \mid B,\, C) \;\propto\; f(B \mid A,\, C)\, \cdot\, f(A \mid C). \;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{First instinct: treat $y_{1:t}$ as a single blob $B$.}} Naive vanilla Bayes ($C = \emptyset$, $B = y_{1:t}$):
\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{f(y_{1:t} \mid \theta_t)}_{(\star)}\, \cdot\, f(\theta_t). \]
The factor $(\star) = f(y_{1:t} \mid \theta_t)$ does not simplify, is not Markov! 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The fix: split the conditioner into background $+$ new datum.}} Don't lump $y_{1:t}$ as one blob; split it:
\[ y_{1:t} \;=\; \underbrace{y_{1:t-1}}_{\text{background } C \text{ (already conditioned on yesterday)}} \;\cup\; \underbrace{y_t}_{\text{new datum } B}. \]
Now apply the boxed conditional Bayes with $A = \theta_t$, $B = y_t$, $C = y_{1:t-1}$:
\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_t,\, y_{1:t-1}) \;\propto\; \underbrace{f(y_t \mid \theta_t,\, y_{1:t-1})\,}_{f(y_t \mid \theta_t)} \cdot\, f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \]

 $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$ is your belief about $\theta_t$ \emph{before seeing $y_t$, after having processed $y_{1:t-1}$}. 



Recalling that a bayesian forecat is: 
\[ P(\, a \le \theta \le b \mid y \,) \;=\; \int_{a}^{b} f(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta \;=\; 1 - \alpha. \]
Now $y$ is fixed (the observed data) and $\theta$ is the random variable; the probability is over the posterior $f(\theta \mid y)$.

By Markov:
\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t-1}) \;=\; \int f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})\, f(\theta_{t-1} \mid y_{1:t-1})\, d\theta_{t-1}, \]
"Today's predicted state distribution = average (intergal) of the transition probabilities form yesterday to today * yesterday's posterior (second term, where you were yesterday)

\emph{Equivalent batch form (textbook / iid case).} When $\theta$ is a \textbf{static} parameter and observations are conditionally iid given $\theta$, you can write the posterior in one shot using all data and the original prior:
\[ f(\theta \mid y_{1:T}) \;\propto\; f(y_{1:T} \mid \theta) \cdot f(\theta) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{iid}}\; \prod_{t=1}^{T} f(y_t \mid \theta) \cdot f(\theta). \]
Note: there is no iid with a time-varying $\theta_t$, and there is no identical distribution either (each $y_t$ has its own $\theta_t$).


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. State Prediction}}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. State prediction} $\;\;f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$.} \emph{Where will the hidden state be $h$ steps from now?} Just keep applying the transition kernel, no new evidence:
\[ f(\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \int f(\theta_{t+1} \mid \theta_t)\, \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})\,}_{\text{obtained by filtering}} d\theta_t \]
and recursively
\[ f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \int f(\theta_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h-1})\, f(\theta_{t+h-1} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h-1}. \]
i obtain this one step per time, so first i predict h+1 then h+2 etc. State h means h iterations. 


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. Observation Prediction}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{PREDICTION --- how Bayesian concepts give us all the formulas}}

**Intro**
\emph{Where does the predictive density come from?} By the definition of a conditional density (chain rule applied to the joint of $T+1$ observations):
\[ f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \frac{f(y_{1:T+1})}{f(y_{1:T})}. \]
This is the natural starting point, BUT SAME AS BEFORE:  \emph{both} densities on the right are usually intractable directly --- each requires integrating the full joint over all latent quantities. The trick is to introduce $\theta$ (parameter or state) into the picture and marginalise it out instead, which gives the closed posterior-predictive form below. 

**General version (textbook posterior predictive)**
 For observed data $y_{1:T}$, future observation $y_{T+1}$, and latent quantity $\theta$ (parameter or state):
\[ \boxed{\; f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \int f(y_{T+1},\, \theta \mid y_{1:T})\, d\theta \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{*}}\; \int f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}, \theta)\, f(\theta \mid y_{1:T})\, d\theta. \; = \; \int f(y_{T+1} \mid \theta_{T+1})\, \underbrace{f(\theta_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T})}_{\text{need to retrive this with filtering and}} d\theta_{T+1}. \;} \]
*you can always ask to yourself, when y takes this value, what value x takes?

Note the integration variabel must watch what's varying in the integrand. 

\emph{Reading.} **KEY**:  For each candidate value of the contemporaneous state $\theta_{T+1}$, the emission gives a forecast $f(y_{T+1} \mid \theta_{T+1})$; we average these forecasts, weighted by how plausible each $\theta_{T+1}$ is given the data we have already seen ($f(\theta_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T})$, the predicted-state distribution).



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Multi-step ahead Observation prediction} $\;\;f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$.} \emph{What value will we observe $h$ steps from now?} Marginalise the future state out of the joint $(y_{t+h}, \theta_{t+h})$:
\[ f(y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \int f(y_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h})\, f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h}. \]
\emph{Reading.} Plug each candidate state $\theta_{t+h}$ into the emission to get a forecast distribution conditional on that state; weight by how likely that state is given the data so far; integrate. This is the \textbf{posterior predictive} from the Bayesian-statistics snippet, applied to the SSM.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4. Smoothing and Decoding}}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4. Smoothing} $\;\;f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T})$.} \emph{Looking back, what was the state at time $t$ given all data including the future?} Bayes again, this time using future data to refine our belief about $\theta_t$:
\[ f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t}) \;\cdot\; \frac{f(y_{t+1:T} \mid \theta_t)}{f(y_{t+1:T} \mid y_{1:t})}, \]
i.e.\ multiply the filtered posterior by the likelihood of the future (given $\theta_t$), then renormalise. The forward--backward algorithm computes this efficiently by running a forward filter then a backward pass.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{5. Decoding (HMM only)} $\;\;\arg\max_{s_{0:T}} f(s_{0:T} \mid y_{1:T})$.} \emph{Most likely path of hidden states.} By Bayes, $f(s_{0:T} \mid y_{1:T}) \propto f(y_{1:T} \mid s_{0:T})\, f(s_{0:T})$, and we already computed both factors when deriving the likelihood (equation $(2)$ in the Estimation snippet). Maximisation over $s_{0:T}$ is done by dynamic programming (Viterbi). For DLMs the joint is Gaussian and the joint mode equals the vector of marginal means --- so smoothing already gives the decoded path.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6. Likelihood (for parameter estimation)} $\;\;f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi)$.} \emph{If the model has unknown parameters $\phi$.} Marginalise out the hidden path:
\[ f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi) \;=\; \int f(y_{1:T},\, \theta_{0:T} \mid \phi)\, d\theta_{0:T}. \]
This is the building block for both:

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist}: maximise over $\phi$ to get the MLE $\hat\phi$.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian}: combine with a prior $\pi(\phi)$ via Bayes' rule, $f(\phi \mid y_{1:T}) \propto f(y_{1:T} \mid \phi)\, \pi(\phi)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Putting parameter uncertainty into prediction.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist plug-in.} Take $\hat\phi$, then compute $f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}, \hat\phi)$ by the rules above. \emph{Pretends $\hat\phi$ is the truth} --- forecast bands too narrow.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian posterior predictive.} Integrate out $\phi$:
\[ f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \int f(y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T}, \phi)\, f(\phi \mid y_{1:T})\, d\phi. \]
This is just \emph{Bayes' rule applied twice}: once to get the filtered/predicted state distribution given $\phi$, then again to integrate out the parameter. Forecast bands honestly account for parameter uncertainty.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Worked example (HMM weather/activity).}} The recursion we used in the filtering exercise,
\[ \alpha_t(j) \;=\; \underbrace{b_{j, y_t}}_{\text{likelihood of new obs}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\sum_{i} \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, p_{i,j}}_{\text{prior carried forward}}, \]
is exactly the SSM filtering formula above, with discrete states. The \emph{predict} half (the sum) propagates yesterday's belief through $\mathbf{P}$; the \emph{update} half (the multiplication by $b_{j, y_t}$) is Bayes applied to today's observation.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bottom line.}} There is only one engine: \emph{posterior $\propto$ likelihood $\cdot$ prior}, with marginalisation to remove unwanted variables. Filtering, smoothing, prediction, decoding, MLE, posterior predictive --- each is just that engine pointed at a different conditional or marginal of the SSM joint.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{5. Decoding --- Viterbi detail}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. DECODING}}

Estimate the latent state sequence $s_{1:T}$ given observed $y_{1:T}$ (treat $s_0$ as fixed, and $\phi$ as known or replaced by its MLE).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Local criterion.}} For each $t = 1, \dots, T$, pick the marginally most likely state:
\[ s_t^* \;=\; \arg\max_s \gamma_t(s), \qquad \gamma_t(s) \;\equiv\; P(S_t = s \mid y_{1:T}, \phi). \]
\emph{Issue.} The resulting sequence $s_{1:T}^*$ may include zero-probability transitions ($p_{i,j} = 0$), making the global path infeasible.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Global criterion --- Viterbi.}} Find the path that maximises the joint conditional probability:
\[ \max_{s_{0:T}} P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T, \phi). \]
Given the data, and the parameters, what is the most likely hidden state? 

This conditional probability can be computed using Bayes theorem. However, we can more easily exploit the computations already carried out for the MLE. Notice that
\[ \begin{aligned} & P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T,\, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi) \\ & \underbrace{=}_{\text{chain rule}} P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T, \phi)\, P(Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi), \end{aligned} \]
where the latter factor on the right-hand side does not depend on $s_{0:T}$. Therefore, maximising the conditional joint probability with respect to $s_{0:T}$ is equivalent to maximising the joint probability $P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T,\, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi)$ wrt phi. Now we need to optimize the same thing by $S_{0:T}$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{6. Gaussian Simplification (closed-form predictive)}}


**Closed form in the Gaussian case** 
Recall $Y_{T+1} = \theta + \varepsilon_{T+1}$
**If** the posterior of the latent is Gaussian
\[ \theta \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_T,\, C_T), \qquad  C_T \;=\; \frac{C_0\, \sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + T\, C_0}, \qquad m_T \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2\, m_0 \;+\; T\, C_0\, \bar y}{\sigma^2 + T\, C_0}. \]
The emission is Gaussian with observation noise $\varepsilon_{T+1} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ ($Y_{T+1} = \theta + \varepsilon_{T+1}$ given $\theta$); the predictive distribution evaluates in closed form to
\[ \boxed{\; Y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\bigl(m_T,\; C_T + \sigma^2\bigr). \;} \]

\emph{Variance has two terms, with meanings.}

$\bullet$ $C_T$ --- \emph{parameter / state uncertainty}: we don't know $\theta$ exactly, only the posterior $\mathcal{N}(m_T, C_T)$.

$\bullet$ $\sigma^2$ --- \emph{future observation noise}: even if we knew $\theta$ exactly, $Y_{T+1}$ would still have noise.

Adding them is the Bayesian honesty about uncertainty: forecast bands include both. The frequentist plug-in $Y_{T+1} \mid \hat\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\hat\theta, \sigma^2)$ keeps only the $\sigma^2$ term and produces bands that are too narrow. IT IS SO OBVIOUS THE FREQUENTIST IS WRONG, JUT BECAUSE BEING $\hat \theta$ ESTIMATED it cannot be used as a fixed point. Note frequentists fixed this by a correction for estiamtion uncertainty.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Beyond fixed state --- general DLM closed form.}}

The simple $\mathcal{N}(m_T, C_T + \sigma^2)$ is the \emph{fixed-state} special case. For a general DLM
\[ \theta_t = G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t,\; w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, W), \qquad Y_t = F\, \theta_t + v_t,\; v_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, V), \]
the predictive is still closed-form, but with more terms.

\emph{Step 1 --- predict the state.} Push the filtered posterior through the transition:
\[ \theta_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(a_{T+1},\, R_{T+1}), \qquad a_{T+1} = G\, m_T, \qquad R_{T+1} = G\, C_T\, G^\top + W. \]
\emph{Scalar / local-level case} ($G = 1$): $\;a_{T+1} = m_T,\quad R_{T+1} = C_T + W.$

\emph{Simplest non-trivial $G$ ($G = 2$, scalar state doubles each step):} $\theta_t = 2\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t$. Then $a_{T+1} = 2\, m_T$ (mean doubles) and $R_{T+1} = 4\, C_T + W$ (variance scales by $G^2 = 4$, plus the new innovation $W$). \textbf{Key asymmetry:} $G$ acts \emph{linearly} on the mean but \emph{quadratically} on the variance --- because $\mathrm{Var}(c X) = c^2 \mathrm{Var}(X)$. \emph{Tiny numerical check.} If $m_T = 5,\, C_T = 1,\, W = 3$: $a_{T+1} = 10,\, R_{T+1} = 4 \cdot 1 + 3 = 7$. (An explosive model in practice, but pedagogically clean.)

\emph{2-dimensional $G$ ($G$ a $2 \times 2$ matrix --- local linear trend).} State $\theta_t = (\mu_t,\, \beta_t)^\top$: level $\mu$ and slope $\beta$. Let $G = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ --- the slope $\beta$ is added into the level $\mu$ each step (linear extrapolation), while the slope itself is unchanged. Suppose the filter gives $m_T = (m_\mu,\, m_\beta)^\top$ and $C_T = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} C_{\mu\mu} & C_{\mu\beta} \\ C_{\mu\beta} & C_{\beta\beta} \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.

\emph{Predicted mean.} Multiply $G$ into $m_T$:
\[ a_{T+1} \;=\; G\, m_T \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} m_\mu \\ m_\beta \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} m_\mu + m_\beta \\ m_\beta \end{pmatrix}. \]
Reading: predicted level $=$ current level $+$ current slope (one-step linear extrapolation); predicted slope $=$ slope (unchanged).

\emph{Predicted variance.} Multiply $G$ on both sides of $C_T$:
\[ R_{T+1} \;=\; G\, C_T\, G^\top + W \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} C_{\mu\mu} + 2\, C_{\mu\beta} + C_{\beta\beta} & \;C_{\mu\beta} + C_{\beta\beta} \\ C_{\mu\beta} + C_{\beta\beta} & C_{\beta\beta} \end{pmatrix} + W. \]

\emph{Step 2 --- predict the observation.} Push the predicted state through the emission:
\[ \boxed{\; Y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(f_{T+1},\, Q_{T+1}), \quad f_{T+1} = F\, a_{T+1}, \quad Q_{T+1} = F\, R_{T+1}\, F^\top + V. \;} \]
\emph{Scalar / local-level case} ($F = 1$, $V = \sigma^2$): $\;f_{T+1} = a_{T+1} = m_T,\quad Q_{T+1} = R_{T+1} + \sigma^2 = C_T + W + \sigma^2.$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{7. Posterior Mean and Precision (algebraic form)}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Posterior precision $1/C_n$.}} The precision \emph{adds}:
\[ \underbrace{\frac{1}{C_n}}_{\text{posterior precision}} \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{C_0}}_{\text{prior precision}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{n}{\sigma^2}}_{\text{data precision}}. \]
The lower the variance of Cn th ebetter! Because both terms are non-negative, $1/C_n \ge 1/C_0$ always --- the posterior is \emph{always} at least as precise as the prior. Even poor-quality data (large $\sigma^2$) adds some information, just less of it. Sharper data ($\sigma^2$ small) or more data ($n$ large) makes the posterior sharper.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Posterior mean $m_n$ as a weighted average.}} Rewrite $m_n$:
\[ m_n \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{1/C_0}{1/C_0 + n/\sigma^2}}_{\text{prior weight}} \cdot m_0 \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{n/\sigma^2}{1/C_0 + n/\sigma^2}}_{\text{data weight}} \cdot \bar y. \]
$m_n$ is a convex combination of the \emph{prior mean} $m_0 = E[\theta]$ and the \emph{sample mean} $\bar y$, with weights proportional to the respective precisions (frequentist would just have used the sample mean).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{8. Worked Example 1 --- RW + noise, fixed state}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{WORKED EXAMPLE --- RW + noise with fixed hidden state}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setup.}} The local-level state-space model with state-noise variance fixed to $W = 0$ (so $w_t = 0$ a.s.\ and the state is constant: $\theta_t = \theta_0 \equiv \theta$ for all $t$):

$\bullet$ \emph{State equation (degenerate random walk):} $\theta_t \;=\; \theta_{t-1},\qquad \theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, C_0).$

$\bullet$ \emph{Observation equation:} $Y_t \;=\; \theta + \varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2),\quad \{\varepsilon_t\} \perp \theta.$

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Goal.}} Compute the posterior $f(\theta \mid y_{1:n})$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Reminder --- Gaussian density (kernel form).}} A $\mathcal{N}(m,\, C)$ density evaluated at $x$ (mean $m$, variance $C$) is
\[ \mathcal{N}(x;\, m,\, C) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi C}} \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{(x - m)^2}{2 C}\Bigr). \]
For matching coefficients, we will repeatedly use the kernel-in-$\theta$ form (everything not involving $\theta$ goes into the normalising constant):
\[ \mathcal{N}(\theta;\, m,\, C) \;\stackrel{\theta}{\propto}\; \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[\theta^2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{C} \;-\; 2\theta \cdot \tfrac{m}{C}\bigr]\Bigr). \]

\begin{tabular}{l|l|l}
Step & Non-recursive (batch) & Recursive (one-step-at-a-time) \\
\hline
\emph{Bayes setup} & iid factorises the likelihood: \;$f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \propto \prod_{t=1}^{n} f(y_t \mid \theta) \cdot \pi(\theta).$ &\;$f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \propto f(y_n \mid \theta_n) \cdot f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n-1}) $ with $f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n-1}) = \mathcal{N}(m_{n-1}, C_{n-1})$:  \\
\hline
\emph{Step 1 - plug in Gaussians} & $f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \propto \exp\!\bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{t=1}^{n}(y_t - \theta)^2\bigr) \cdot \exp\!\bigl(-\tfrac{(\theta - m_0)^2}{2 C_0}\bigr).$ & $f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \propto \exp\!\bigl(-\tfrac{(y_n - \theta_n)^2}{2\sigma^2}\bigr) \cdot \exp\!\bigl(-\tfrac{(\theta_n - m_{n-1})^2}{2 C_{n-1}}\bigr).$ \\
\hline
\emph{Step 2 - collect $\theta^2,\, \theta$ terms} & $f(\theta \mid y_{1:n}) \stackrel{\theta}{\propto} \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl[\theta^2\bigl(\tfrac{1}{C_0} + \tfrac{n}{\sigma^2}\bigr) - 2\theta\bigl(\tfrac{m_0}{C_0} + \tfrac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\bigr)\Bigr]\Bigr).$ & $f(\theta_n \mid y_{1:n}) \stackrel{\theta_n}{\propto} \exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl[\theta_n^2\bigl(\tfrac{1}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}\bigr) - 2\theta_n\bigl(\tfrac{m_{n-1}}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{y_n}{\sigma^2}\bigr)\Bigr]\Bigr).$ \\
\hline
\emph{Step 3 - match the kernel} $(m, C)$ & $\tfrac{1}{C_n} = \tfrac{1}{C_0} + \tfrac{n}{\sigma^2}; \quad m_n = C_n\bigl(\tfrac{m_0}{C_0} + \tfrac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\bigr).$ \;Equivalently: \;$C_n = \tfrac{C_0\, \sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + n\, C_0}, \quad m_n = \tfrac{\sigma^2\, m_0 + n\, C_0\, \bar y}{\sigma^2 + n\, C_0}.$ & $\tfrac{1}{C_n} = \tfrac{1}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}; \quad m_n = C_n\bigl(\tfrac{m_{n-1}}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{y_n}{\sigma^2}\bigr).$ \;Equivalently: \;$C_n = \tfrac{C_{n-1}\, \sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + C_{n-1}},\quad m_n = \tfrac{\sigma^2\, m_{n-1} + C_{n-1}\, y_n}{\sigma^2 + C_{n-1}}.$ \\
\hline
\emph{Result} & $\boxed{\; \theta \mid y_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_n,\, C_n) \;}$ with the closed-form $(m_n, C_n)$ above. & $\boxed{\; \theta_n \mid y_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_n,\, C_n) \;}$ obtained by iterating the recursion $n$ times from $(m_0, C_0)$. \\
\end{tabular}

\emph{Equivalence.} The two routes yield the same $(m_n, C_n)$: telescoping the precision recursion $\tfrac{1}{C_n} = \tfrac{1}{C_{n-1}} + \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}$ gives $\tfrac{1}{C_n} = \tfrac{1}{C_0} + \tfrac{n}{\sigma^2}$ (the batch formula); similarly for $m_n$. Batch $=$ one Bayes step on the full product; recursive $=$ $n$ Bayes steps on individual factors. Same answer.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Forecast $Y_{n+1}$ (after filtering).}} With the just-obtained posterior $\theta_n \mid y_{1:n} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_n, C_n)$ and $Y_{n+1} = \theta_{n+1} + \varepsilon_{n+1} = \theta_n + \varepsilon_{n+1}$ (fixed state), sum of independent Gaussians gives
\[ \boxed{\; Y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_n,\; C_n + \sigma^2). \;} \]
Standard one-step-ahead predictive: mean $f_{n+1} = m_n$, variance $Q_{n+1} = C_n + \sigma^2$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Prediction-error correction (Kalman) form.}} Algebraically simplifying the precision-blend formula for $m_n$ (recursive column) gives the interpretable Kalman update
\[ \boxed{\; m_n \;=\; m_{n-1} + K_n\, \underbrace{(y_n - m_{n-1})}_{e_n \,=\, \text{prediction error}}, \qquad K_n \;=\; \frac{C_{n-1}}{C_{n-1} + \sigma^2}. \;} \]
$e_n = y_n - m_{n-1}$ is the innovation. $K_n$ goes up (we trust the new observation more) when reliability is high.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Two readings of the Kalman gain $K_n$.}}

$\bullet$ \textbf{(1) Ratio of variances (signal-to-total).} Of the total variability of $Y_n$, what fraction comes from \emph{state uncertainty} (informative about $\theta_n$) vs \emph{observation noise} (uninformative)? State dominates $\Rightarrow K_n \to 1$; noise dominates $\Rightarrow K_n \to 0$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{9. Worked Example 2 --- RW + noise, dynamic state ($W > 0$)}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{WORKED EXAMPLE --- RW + noise (DYNAMIC state, $W > 0$).}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Setup.}} Full local-level state-space model, state \emph{not} fixed (random walk with non-zero variance):

$\bullet$ \emph{State equation (random walk):} $\;\theta_t \;=\; \theta_{t-1} + w_t,\qquad w_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, W),\quad W > 0,$ with $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0,\, C_0)$.

$\bullet$ \emph{Observation equation:} $\;Y_t \;=\; \theta_t + \varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, V),\quad \{\varepsilon_t\} \perp \{w_t\} \perp \theta_0.$

\emph{DLM tuple (specialisation of the general template):} $\;G = 1,\;\; F = 1,\;\; W = W,\;\; V = V.$ State is 1D; everything stays scalar.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Suppose we have already filtered up to time $T$.}} After processing $y_{1:T}$, the filter outputs the current state posterior
\[ \theta_T \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_T,\, C_T). \]
Now run the two-step Gaussian-simplification recipe to forecast $\theta_{T+1}$ and $Y_{T+1}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 1 --- Predict the state $f(\theta_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T})$.}}

Push the filtered posterior through the transition. Generic formula: $a_{T+1} = G\, m_T$, $R_{T+1} = G\, C_T\, G^\top + W$. With $G = 1$ this collapses to
\[ \boxed{\; \theta_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(a_{T+1},\, R_{T+1}), \qquad a_{T+1} \;=\; m_T, \qquad R_{T+1} \;=\; C_T + W. \;} \]

\emph{Reading.} The predicted mean is just $m_T$ (RW has no drift). The predicted variance is the filtered variance \emph{plus} a fresh chunk $W$ injected by the transition: even if you knew $\theta_T$ exactly, $\theta_{T+1}$ would still wander by $\mathcal{N}(0, W)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 2 --- Predict the observation $f(Y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T})$.}}

Push the predicted state through the emission. Generic formula: $f_{T+1} = F\, a_{T+1}$, $Q_{T+1} = F\, R_{T+1}\, F^\top + V$. With $F = 1$, $V = V$:
\[ \boxed{\; Y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(f_{T+1},\, Q_{T+1}), \qquad f_{T+1} \;=\; m_T, \qquad Q_{T+1} \;=\; C_T + W + V. \;} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Three sources of forecast uncertainty in $Q_{T+1}$.}} Read off the decomposition:
\[ Q_{T+1} \;=\; \underbrace{C_T}_{\substack{\text{(1) state posterior} \\ \text{uncertainty (carried)}}} \;+\; \underbrace{W}_{\substack{\text{(2) new state innovation} \\ \text{(only present if } W > 0)}} \;+\; \underbrace{V}_{\substack{\text{(3) observation} \\ \text{noise}}}. \]

$\bullet$ \emph{(1) $C_T$ --- posterior uncertainty about the current state.} After all $T$ filtering steps, we still don't know $\theta_T$ exactly --- this is the residual variance from filtering. Carried forward unchanged because $G = 1$.

$\bullet$ \emph{(2) $W$ --- new state innovation.} The walk's own randomness between $T$ and $T+1$: even knowing $\theta_T$ exactly, the next state is $\theta_T + w_{T+1}$, $w_{T+1} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, W)$. \textbf{This term is the new entry compared to the fixed-state case.}

$\bullet$ \emph{(3) $V$ --- observation noise.} The measurement noise on $Y_{T+1}$, unavoidable even if you knew $\theta_{T+1}$ exactly.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Fixed-state special case ($W = 0$) recovers the previous worked example.}}

Setting $W = 0$ kills term (2):
\[ a_{T+1} = m_T, \qquad R_{T+1} = C_T, \qquad f_{T+1} = m_T, \qquad Q_{T+1} = C_T + V. \]
Identical to the fixed-state worked example: the state can't change, so the only sources of forecast variance are filter residual uncertainty $C_T$ and observation noise $V$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Full filter recursion at time $T+1$.}} For completeness: once $y_{T+1}$ arrives, apply the Kalman update with $R_{T+1}$ as the predicted-prior variance:

\emph{Predict (above):} $a_{T+1} = m_T,\quad R_{T+1} = C_T + W$.

\emph{Update:} blend predicted prior with new datum.
\[ \frac{1}{C_{T+1}} \;=\; \frac{1}{R_{T+1}} + \frac{1}{V}, \qquad m_{T+1} \;=\; C_{T+1}\Bigl(\tfrac{a_{T+1}}{R_{T+1}} + \tfrac{y_{T+1}}{V}\Bigr). \]

\emph{Kalman gain form (equivalent):}
\[ m_{T+1} \;=\; a_{T+1} + K_{T+1}\, \underbrace{(y_{T+1} - f_{T+1})}_{e_{T+1}\,=\,\text{innovation}}, \qquad K_{T+1} \;=\; \frac{R_{T+1}}{R_{T+1} + V} \;=\; \frac{C_T + W}{C_T + W + V}. \]
$K_{T+1} \to 1$ when the state is much more uncertain than the observation noise (trust the new datum); $K_{T+1} \to 0$ in the opposite regime.

\emph{Signal-to-noise ratio.} The book (Petris--Petrone--Campagnoli, p.\ 39) names $W / V$ as the SNR: it is the single dimensionless number controlling how reactive the filter is. High SNR $\Rightarrow K \to 1$ (filter tracks every wiggle); low SNR $\Rightarrow K \to 0$ (filter smooths heavily, treating data as noise around an essentially-constant state).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{$h$-step forecast.}} Iterate Step 1 forward $h$ times. With $G = 1$: $a_{T+h} = m_T$ for all $h$, and $R_{T+h} = C_T + h\, W$ (each step adds $W$). Then $Q_{T+h} = R_{T+h} + V = C_T + h W + V$:
\[ \boxed{\; Y_{T+h} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(m_T,\; C_T + h\, W + V). \;} \]
Forecast bands fan out linearly in $h$ --- the hallmark of a random-walk signal.

trash.title: State Prediction
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. State prediction} $\;\;f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$.} \emph{Where will the hidden state be $h$ steps from now?} Just keep applying the transition kernel, no new evidence:
\[ f(\theta_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \int f(\theta_{t+1} \mid \theta_t)\, \underbrace{f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})\,}_{\text{obtained by filtering}} d\theta_t \]
and recursively
\[ f(\theta_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t}) \;=\; \int f(\theta_{t+h} \mid \theta_{t+h-1})\, f(\theta_{t+h-1} \mid y_{1:t})\, d\theta_{t+h-1}. \]
i obtain this one step per time, so first i predict h+1 then h+2 etc. State h means h iterations.

trash.title: Gaussian simplification
trash.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Beyond fixed state --- general DLM closed form.}}

The simple $\mathcal{N}(m_T, C_T + \sigma^2)$ is the \emph{fixed-state} special case. For a general DLM
\[ \theta_t = G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t,\; w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, W), \qquad Y_t = F\, \theta_t + v_t,\; v_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, V), \]
the predictive is still closed-form, but with more terms.

\emph{Step 1 --- predict the state.} Push the filtered posterior through the transition:
\[ \theta_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(a_{T+1},\, R_{T+1}), \qquad a_{T+1} = G\, m_T, \qquad R_{T+1} = G\, C_T\, G^\top + W. \]
\emph{Scalar / local-level case} ($G = 1$): $\;a_{T+1} = m_T,\quad R_{T+1} = C_T + W.$

\emph{Simplest non-trivial $G$ ($G = 2$, scalar state doubles each step):} $\theta_t = 2\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t$. Then $a_{T+1} = 2\, m_T$ (mean doubles) and $R_{T+1} = 4\, C_T + W$ (variance scales by $G^2 = 4$, plus the new innovation $W$). \textbf{Key asymmetry:} $G$ acts \emph{linearly} on the mean but \emph{quadratically} on the variance --- because $\mathrm{Var}(c X) = c^2 \mathrm{Var}(X)$. \emph{Tiny numerical check.} If $m_T = 5,\, C_T = 1,\, W = 3$: $a_{T+1} = 10,\, R_{T+1} = 4 \cdot 1 + 3 = 7$. (An explosive model in practice, but pedagogically clean.)

\emph{2-dimensional $G$ ($G$ a $2 \times 2$ matrix --- local linear trend).} State $\theta_t = (\mu_t,\, \beta_t)^\top$: level $\mu$ and slope $\beta$. Let $G = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ --- the slope $\beta$ is added into the level $\mu$ each step (linear extrapolation), while the slope itself is unchanged. Suppose the filter gives $m_T = (m_\mu,\, m_\beta)^\top$ and $C_T = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} C_{\mu\mu} & C_{\mu\beta} \\ C_{\mu\beta} & C_{\beta\beta} \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$.

\emph{Predicted mean.} Multiply $G$ into $m_T$:
\[ a_{T+1} \;=\; G\, m_T \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} m_\mu \\ m_\beta \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} m_\mu + m_\beta \\ m_\beta \end{pmatrix}. \]
Reading: predicted level $=$ current level $+$ current slope (one-step linear extrapolation); predicted slope $=$ slope (unchanged).

\emph{Predicted variance.} Multiply $G$ on both sides of $C_T$:
\[ R_{T+1} \;=\; G\, C_T\, G^\top + W \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} C_{\mu\mu} + 2\, C_{\mu\beta} + C_{\beta\beta} & \;C_{\mu\beta} + C_{\beta\beta} \\ C_{\mu\beta} + C_{\beta\beta} & C_{\beta\beta} \end{pmatrix} + W. \]

\emph{Step 2 --- predict the observation.} Push the predicted state through the emission:
\[ \boxed{\; Y_{T+1} \mid y_{1:T} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(f_{T+1},\, Q_{T+1}), \quad f_{T+1} = F\, a_{T+1}, \quad Q_{T+1} = F\, R_{T+1}\, F^\top + V. \;} \]
\emph{Scalar / local-level case} ($F = 1$, $V = \sigma^2$): $\;f_{T+1} = a_{T+1} = m_T,\quad Q_{T+1} = R_{T+1} + \sigma^2 = C_T + W + \sigma^2.$
